the seat believes. That is the standing lesson of this register applied to the
seat that keeps writing it down.
## INC-2026-10-12-the-press-had-no-degraded-path-and-the-week-got-no-issue — the product's one output, missing, with every machine involved reporting correctly (2026-10-12, engineer seat, second run)

**Observed by:** the engineer seat's second run of 2026-10-12, 20:40 UTC,
running `python3 tools/delivery_health.py` as the first observation step of an
ordinary OODA cycle. The press surface read `FAILING  press  the newest issue
is 2026-W40 and 2026-W41 has ended; 1 issue(s) missing`, and the live site
agreed: `GET /library/2026-W41` returns 404, `/library/2026-W40` returns 200,
and `/library` lists `2026-W39` and `2026-W40` and nothing newer. The Monday
09:00 UTC cron had fired about eleven hours earlier.

**What happened.** The press walked its fallback list, every entry was refused,
and the week got no issue. The arithmetic, printed by the org's own guard on
every run since 2026-09-24:

| rank | model | the request | the ceiling | verdict |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | kimi-k2.6 | 104,323 tokens | 222,822 usable | fits, and did not answer |
| 2 | openai/gpt-oss-120b | 104,323 tokens | 6,800 usable | over by 97,523 |
| 3 | qwen/qwen3.8-27b | 104,323 tokens | 6,800 usable | over by 97,523 |
| 4 | openai/gpt-oss-20b | 104,323 tokens | 6,800 usable | over by 97,523 |

`prompts/digest.md` is 1,919 lines, which is 43,750 tokens before a single
claim is attached, so the prompt and the output reservation alone are 67,750
tokens against a free-tier minute of 8,000. `budget.fit_payload` says in its
own words that no payload selection can rescue this. The three Groq entries
have therefore never been able to print, and the comment beside
`FALLBACK_MODELS` has said as much since incident 24: they are there "for the
day the prompt gets shorter or a ceiling moves. A last resort that prints
something small beats a last resort that does not exist."

Nothing was broken on 2026-10-12. Every component behaved as specified. The
guard printed `DOES NOT FIT` three times, `write_digest` moved down the list
correctly, `PressCannotPrint` was raised with the whole trail, and
`notify_owner` mailed it. What did not exist was the thing the comment was
waiting for, so the honest statement of the defect is that the press's
degraded path was a list rather than a path, for 18 days, and the week the
primary went quiet is the week that discovered it.

**The repeat, which is why this is filed.** The class is
`a fallback that cannot take the request is not a fallback`, and the org has
now met it four times:

- incident 22, 2026-09-24: the press's single model refused a request larger
  than its minute. Fixed by sizing the request.
- `INC-2026-09-24-press-provider-migration`: the fallback list existed and
  three of its four failures were on paths nothing had exercised.
- `INC-2026-10-11` and `INC-2026-10-12-the-free-tiers-day...`: the corpus
  stages' fallback was configured and unpaced, then paced and unshared.
- this entry: the press's fallback was configured and arithmetically
  impossible, which is the same defect with the smallest possible symptom,
  one missing artifact and no error anywhere.

`budget.check_request` has printed the evidence for this entry on every CI run
for 18 days. A guard whose output nothing is required to act on is a guard
that documents an outage in advance.

**What shipped with this entry.** `prompts/digest-short.md`, a generator prompt
sized to the minute the free tier actually publishes;
`budget.short_issue_room`, which derives the output reservation and the payload
allowance from that published minute rather than choosing them;
`budget.check_short_issue`, which fails the deploy when no model off the
primary's provider can print even the short edition; and `weekly.print_issue`,
which reaches for the short edition only when the full one fits nothing. The
issue says it is short, in a line the press adds rather than the generator, and
the owner gets `ALARM_SUBJECT_SHORT_EDITION` when it is what went out.

**What it does not fix.** The short prompt carries a handful of the 103 entries
in `docs/voice/ban-list.md`, because the rest do not fit in a 6,800-token
request. The short edition is therefore the lesser issue by construction, and
which rules survive is an editorial judgment that belongs to the writer seat
rather than to the arithmetic in this diff.

## INC-2026-10-12-the-deploy-ladder-refuses-the-fix-for-the-outage-it-is-in — gate 3 asks the broken thing for permission to deploy its own repair (2026-10-12, engineer seat, second run)

**Observed by:** the same run, reading the three commands the previous run's
urgent ledger entry had addressed to the owner, and then reading what those
commands do.

**What happened.** Two merged pull requests, #270 and #275, sized the
fallback's minute and the fallback's day so that the corpus could carry itself
with the primary absent. Both were inert, because a Modal app is deployed by a
command and no seat holds the token. The ledger said so and called it three
commands. The commands cannot complete.

`tools/deploy_gate.py --app all --plan` prints each chain as
`python3 pipeline/budget.py && modal run <app>::preflight && modal run
<app>::rehearse && modal deploy <app>`, and `rehearse` ends like this in
`pipeline/triage.py` and `pipeline/interpret.py` both:

```python
if model != MODELS[0]:
    raise client.NoModelAnswered(
        f"the rehearsal was answered by {model}, not by {MODELS[0]}, which "
        "is what the deploy installs. A receipt from a fallback is not a "
        "receipt: fix the head of the list before deploying, because "
        "tomorrow's cron meets it first.")
```

`MODELS[0]` is `kimi-k2.6`. The primary was not answering, which is the whole
reason there was a fix to deploy: `tools/delivery_health.py` reported triage
answering on `openai/gpt-oss-120b` and interpret on `qwen/qwen3.8-27b` the same
morning. So every corpus rehearsal was answered by a fallback, every chain
stopped at the third `&&`, and the stall entered its sixth day with its cure
sitting in `main`. The press chain stopped one rung earlier, at `preflight`,
for the reason the entry above gives.

The gate is not wrong. It is right on every day except the one day its own
subject is the outage, and on that day it inverts: refusing the deploy is what
keeps the outage. No seat had noticed, because the seat that writes the fix is
not the seat that runs the command, and the command's refusal is only ever read
by the owner.

**The repeat.** The class is L-A16, `configured is not in effect`, which the
ledger already cited this week for the undeployed fixes. This entry is the
layer under it: not only is configured not in effect, the path from configured
to in effect had a gate that could not open. `INC-2026-10-07-a-charter-
dispatched-thirteen-runs-at-work-that-was-already-built` is the same shape in a
different register, work that exists and cannot be reached.

**What shipped with this entry.** `budget.head_receipt`, one text and one
argument for all four gates, and `--allow-fallback` on
`pipeline/triage.py::rehearse`, `pipeline/interpret.py::rehearse` and
`pipeline/weekly.py::rehearse`. It refuses by default, exactly as before, and
the refusal now names the hatch. With the hatch open it prints what it forgave
and the receipt says the degraded path was what was proved. Modelled on
`pipeline/distill.py::rehearse --allow-abstract-only`, which has carried this
shape since 2026-09-27 and is the reason distill was the one corpus app whose
chain could have completed today.

## INC-2026-10-12-the-writers-cap-raise-landed-with-no-smoke-run — a `--max-turns` change whose first execution will be a scheduled run (2026-10-12, engineer seat, second run, reported not fixed)

**Observed by:** the engineer seat's machinery-diff check, which is step 0 of
this seat's "check the register before you ship" clause and the reason that
clause exists.

**What the diff showed.** `git log --since="36 hours ago" -- .github/ pipeline/`
returns two real changes. The first is pull request #275, this morning's
fallback-share work, explained by its own description and assessed by that run.
The second is pull request #278, merged at 20:03 UTC today, one line:

```
-  claude_args: "--max-turns 150 --permission-mode bypassPermissions --model claude-opus-5"
+  claude_args: "--max-turns 225 --permission-mode bypassPermissions --model claude-opus-5"
```

**Question one is answered and question two is not.** A merged pull request
explains it, in full and well: two exhaustions six days apart, both at
`num_turns 151`, the second losing commits it had never pushed, and L-X3 as
amended giving the step of half again rather than a doubling. That is the
reasoning the law asks for. What `gh run list --workflow=agent-writer.yml`
shows is that the newest writer run is 2026-10-11 19:46 UTC on `39a8062`,
which is before the raise. No run has executed under the new cap.

`docs/agents/runtime-changes.md` puts `claude_args` and `--max-turns` on its
list by name and says turn caps are on it deliberately, "because they look like
numbers rather than machinery, and incident 15 is a day of six failures caused
by numbers." Its closing line is the test applied here: any runtime change with
no smoke run behind it in `gh run list` is a finding. The next scheduled writer
run will be this change's first execution, which is the one thing that law
exists to prevent.

**The proportion, stated rather than left to be inferred.** The change is
monotonic and permissive, it moves one integer up, and the most likely outcome
is that it simply works. This entry is not a prediction that it will fail. It
is the finding the law asks for, filed because the law has no exemption for a
change that looks obviously correct, and because the same seat's own cap was
the subject of `INC-2026-10-09-the-writer-hit-the-cap-its-own-raise-queued-
five-days-earlier` three days ago, which makes this the second cap event in
four days and a repeat under the standing rule at the top of this file.

**Not fixed, deliberately.** This seat cannot push a workflow file, so the
remedy is a `workflow_dispatch` of the writer seat before its next scheduled
run, which is the owner's. Reported in one line in the pull request that
carries this entry.
## INC-2026-10-13-the-uncovered-set-grew-again-and-this-time-it-is-the-payments-guards — the sixth day of a staged fix nobody can apply, and the two files it leaves silent now guard money (2026-10-13, engineer seat)

**Observed by:** the engineer seat's scheduled run of 2026-10-13, when
`tests/test_ci_coverage.py::test_the_uncovered_set_has_not_grown` failed on
the two test files this run wrote.

**What happened.** This is a repeat, recorded because the standing rule at
the top of this file admits no judgment call, and the repeat is of
`INC-2026-10-02-markdown-suite-claims-a-ci-step-it-never-had`. The shape is
unchanged: a seat writes a test file, the live `.github/workflows/checks.yml`
runs fourteen named steps and none of them is the new file, and no agent
token in this organization may write a workflow, so the only available move
is to pin the file in `UNCOVERED` and say why.

```
$ python3 -m pytest tests/ -q
E       AssertionError: 2 test file(s) run in no workflow and are not pinned:
E           tests/polar.test.mjs
E           tests/test_polar.py

$ python3 tools/ci_coverage.py --workflows .github/workflows-pending
52 of 52 test files run in CI
```

The pin is in this run's diff with its reason, which is what the gate asks
for, so nothing here is a rule broken. What makes it worth an entry rather
than a line in a pull request is the second number. The staged replacement
has been correct and unapplied since 2026-10-07, which is six days, and the
set it would empty has grown twice in that window. Item 17 of
`docs/agents/pending-workflow-changes.md` is measured, verified against the
live file's anchors, and runs all 52 files including these two.

**Why these two are not like the other thirty-four pins.** Every other line
in that set costs a red run that somebody notices later. These two hold the
signature check on `/api/polar-webhook`, which is the only thing standing
between a stranger with a forged payload and the paid surfaces, and the gate
in `site/lib/entitlement.js` that decides who may open one. A regression in
either reports nothing on any pull request. The first evidence would be a
sale that granted nothing, or access granted to somebody who did not buy.

This run also found the first instance of exactly that class of defect, in a
file that has been on `main` since 2026-09-19 and is covered by a test which
asserts it: `isEntitled` in `site/lib/account-core.js` opens the paid tier on
`digest_comp`, and `site/lib/waitlist-core.js` sets that flag on every free
signup. A passing test pinned it. Filed as the `urgent` ledger entry of
today's date rather than fixed here, because it decides what a comped friend
is entitled to and that is the owner's call.

**Measured, not inferred, after the pull request was opened.** The entry
above was written from the gate's own failure, which says these two files
run in no workflow. The pull request then said something stronger:

```
$ gh pr checks 285
no checks reported on the 'engineer/2026-10-13-polar-spine' branch
```

Not a red tick. No tick. `checks.yml`'s `paths:` filter lists fourteen test
files by name plus `pipeline/**`, `skills/**`, `db/schema.sql` and
`site/lib/skill-provenance.js`, and a diff of five new `site/` files, two new
`tests/` files and three documents matches none of them. The filter is
behaving exactly as written. So the whole payments layer, including the
signature check on `/api/polar-webhook`, is proposed for merge with no
continuous integration behind it at all, and the only evidence that the 1,315
tests pass is a seat's own transcript. That is the state item 17 fixes, and
it is worse than "a file nobody runs": the pull request does not even claim
to have been checked, so there is no red for a reviewer to notice.

**The fix, and the part a seat can reach.** None of it. Applying item 17
needs a `workflows` permission no seat holds. The reachable half is already
done: the measurement exists, the gate pins the set so it can shrink and
cannot grow silently, and this entry is the sixth day's evidence that the
cost of not applying it is no longer only a red tick.

**A third file joined the pin the same day (added by this seat's third run of
2026-10-13, 2026-10-13).** The entry above counts two growths in six days.
There are three, and the third is six hours old:
`tests/test_institution_backfill.py`, written by the institution backfill run,
caught by the same gate on the same assertion and pinned with the same reason.
The number that matters is not three, it is the rate: the set grew twice in the
six days before today and once more today, so on the day this entry was filed
the growth rate went up rather than down.

```
$ python3 -m pytest tests/ -q
E       AssertionError: 1 test file(s) run in no workflow and are not pinned:
E           tests/test_institution_backfill.py

$ python3 tools/ci_coverage.py --report-only
14 of 53 test files run in CI

$ python3 tools/ci_coverage.py --report-only --workflows .github/workflows-pending
53 of 53 test files run in CI
```

One difference worth recording, because it is the opposite of the "no checks at
all" finding above. This run's diff touches `pipeline/**` and `db/schema.sql`,
both named in the live `paths:` filter, so `checks.yml` does run on this branch
and passed on the commit that carried them. They are the same fourteen steps,
and the forty-one assertions this run wrote are not among them. A pull request
that reports green while the file it added runs nowhere is the harder version of
the problem, because the green tick is the thing a reviewer reads.

**And one measurement note, because it nearly became a false finding here.**
`gh pr checks` reads the head commit only. Run against this pull request four
minutes after a push it answered `no checks reported on the
'engineer/2026-10-13-institution-backfill' branch`, the same sentence quoted
above as evidence for #285, while `gh run list --branch` showed two completed,
successful `checks` runs on the same branch. For #285 the sentence was true and
checked both ways: that branch has no workflow runs at all, by
`gh run list --branch engineer/2026-10-13-polar-spine`, which returns nothing.
For this one it was a queue delay. The two commands answer different questions,
and a seat reporting "no checks" should run both, because L-E11's rule applies
to a guard's absence exactly as it applies to its colour: the smallest true
thing here is "the head commit has no completed check yet", not "this pull
request has no continuous integration".
## INC-2026-10-12-meta-review-proposal-merged-never-deployed — the recursive loop's first merged self-improvement spent a week not running (2026-10-12, research seat)

**Found by:** the research charter's own gate, "check that the file you
are proposing into can reach production", run before spending this
week's one system diff.

**What it found.** `prompts/triage.md` at HEAD is `3ea6485103c3`, which is
commit `fa029bf`, "research 2026-10-05 meta-review: triage reads containment
too narrowly in two places". The deployed prompt is `32252384ecd7`, which is
`ea61cbc` of 2026-09-29.

```sql
select left(prompt_sha,12) sha, count(*), max(created_at)::date from triage_log group by 1;
-- 32252384ecd7 | 8861 | 2026-10-12
```

8,861 rows written against the superseded prompt, the newest of them today.
`deploy_runtime` agrees from the other side: `weekly`, `triage` and
`interpret` all carry `first_seen_at` of 2026-10-05, so no image has been
replaced in seven days.

**The repeat this is.** `INC-2026-09-28-repair-written-never-deployed` is the
general form and this is its fifth instance, after incident 25,
`INC-2026-09-26-interpret-stale-third-sighting`, and
`INC-2026-09-30-triage-runtime-change-with-no-rehearsal`, which is this exact
file and predicted this exact outcome in its own last paragraph: "If that PR
is not merged, `ea61cbc` still needs its own `modal deploy
pipeline/triage.py`." It was the newer commit that ended up waiting.

**What is new, and why it is worth an entry rather than a cross-reference.**
Every prior instance was a pipeline fix or an owner's direct push. This one is
the output of the self-improvement loop itself (ADR-7): a proposal this seat
produced from evidence, reviewed, merged, and never run. O3 KR2 counts "the
meta-review loop merges its first self-improvement PR"; that happened on
2026-10-05 and the merge bought nothing, because the prompt it changed has not
judged a single paper. A loop that closes at the merge and not at the deploy
measures itself on the wrong event.

**It also cost this week's proposal its first choice.** The charter bars
proposing into a file whose deployed sha is stale, for the reason it states:
a second fix stacked behind an undeployed first one reads as progress and
changes nothing. So the triage prompt was barred as a target today even though
the week's evidence pointed at it, and the diff went to
`prompts/interpret.md`, whose deployed sha does equal HEAD. The cost of the
undeployed fix is therefore not only its own absence; it is that the next fix
cannot be written where it is needed.

**No blame in it.** The 2026-10-05 brief checked the three shas and found them
matching main, and said so: "the deploy freeze that made incidents 25 and 26
is over". That was true when it was written. The freeze returned the moment
that run's own PR merged, because a merge is what creates the gap and nothing
closes it automatically.

**What would actually close it** is unchanged from
`INC-2026-09-30-triage-runtime-change-with-no-rehearsal`: a deployed-sha check
that runs on a schedule and fails loudly, rather than six seats inferring it
by hand. The org has now inferred this state by hand six times, twice from
this seat. `tools/delivery_health.py --surface deploy` is most of the
instrument and answers `unknown` today because `distill` and `ingest` have
never recorded a runtime row; the two prompts whose shas *are* recorded could
be compared by it this morning and are not.
## INC-2026-10-04-the-writers-first-cap-out-went-unfiled-until-the-second-one-cost-work — the writer hit `error_max_turns` five days before the loss that got an entry, and nothing here named the first one until the centralizer counted the portfolio (2026-10-04, writer seat, filed 2026-10-13 by the PM seat, refiled from a branch that never merged)

**Observed by:** the PM seat, on a note from `alexandra-systems/exo-centralizer`
reporting that the writer "ran out of turns twice in six days." One of the two,
`INC-2026-10-09-the-writer-hit-the-cap-its-own-raise-queued-five-days-earlier`,
already had an entry here. This one did not, and the gap is the finding.

**What happened.** The writer's scheduled run (`37226048547`, 2026-10-04,
18:51:39Z to 19:17:41Z) ended `"subtype": "error_max_turns"`,
`"is_error": true`, `"num_turns": 151` against `--max-turns 150` in
`.github/workflows/agent-writer.yml` — the identical hard-starvation shape
`docs/agents/turn-caps.md` names, five days before the seat hit it again.
Checked here rather than assumed: the run had pushed real commits as late as
19:16:47Z, one minute before the cap killed it, and the resulting pull
request (`#189`) merged the next day. So this occurrence cost no work, which
is almost certainly why nobody filed it — the no-ship tripwire never fired, and
a failed run with nothing visibly lost reads as nothing, not as evidence.

**Why it is recorded now, nine days late.** `docs/standards/lessons.md`'s L-X3
amendment of 2026-10-12 says plainly that an `error_max_turns` exit is a
finding about the cap and not about the run, regardless of whether that run's
own work survived. This repository's own incident register did not apply that
reading to its own history: the 2026-10-09 entry documents the second,
costly exhaustion in full and never mentions the first, so a reader of this
file alone would have no way to know the writer had already hit the same
wall once. The standard's own portfolio count is what surfaced it, not a run
here.

**Why this entry carries yesterday's date rather than today's.** A PM run on
2026-10-12 filed this exact text on `alexandria-pm/2026-10-12-message-cap-reply`
(PR #279), but that branch went conflicting against `main` and was never
merged. This run found the gap was still open on `main`, confirmed the
pull request's own content was never the problem, and refiled the same entry
here rather than leaving it stranded on a branch nobody will merge. PR #279
is closed as superseded by this one, per the note on it.

**What this run did.** Filed this entry, verified against the run's own log
and the git history in its window rather than taken on the note's word alone.
No rerun — the run is nine days old and its pull request already merged.
No further fix proposed here: the rule, the raise to 225 and the repeat-counter
tool are already merged (`#278`) and the vendored standard, and this entry's
job is only to close the register gap the note pointed at.

**The general point.** A cap hit that costs nothing is still a cap hit, and
"the tripwire didn't fire" is a reason nobody looked, not a reason it didn't
happen. A register that only grows when a failure also destroys work will
keep missing the earlier, cheaper warning every time, which is exactly the
shape L-X3's amendment exists to close.

## INC-2026-10-13-a-generator-gate-read-the-main-clause-and-the-defect-moved-right — the attribution gate was deployed, correct and complete when the issue it guards printed six violations of it, five in a subordinate clause (2026-10-13, writer seat)

**Observed by:** the writer seat's run of 2026-10-13, running the generator's own
attribution gate over the artifact by hand because no issue printed this week and
the gates were the only work left.

**What happened.** `prompts/digest.md` carries a hard gate near the end of its
output checks, present in the deployed file at commit `3bbf430` and therefore
live when 2026-W40 was written. Its words: "Find every sentence whose subject is
a benchmark, a method, a pipeline, a system, a dataset or a paper title, and
whose verb is a verb of research or reporting."

The issue it wrote carries six sentences of that shape and five of the six put
the offending subject in a relative clause, hanging off a main clause the gate
clears on inspection. "Task-adapted low-level VLA policies that reported 86.20%",
"Latent Interface Training, which improves LIBERO-Plus success", "Dynin-Robotics,
which attains 78.4%", "Movement Trend Guidance, which improves mixed-training
performance", "Rethinking On-Policy Distillation II, which argued that one
training example suffices". A writer asked for the SENTENCE's subject answers
with the main clause and stops.

Two of the six also use nouns the gate's own list does not name. "New paired
feedback studies show" and "Ablation shows" are a study and an analysis doing
research, and the list reads benchmark, method, pipeline, system, dataset, paper
title.

**Why this is a repeat and not a discovery.** This is the fourth time a rule in
this generator has been obeyed in the form its specimen had and broken one
position over, and three of the four are already on the ban list with their own
entries. Entry 93: the section turn was banned as a sentence and printed as the
first sentence of each group instead. Entry 94: the grade's WORDS were fixed and
the grade moved to the last position, which nothing was defending. Entry 108: the
cadence rule is read before the title and the period words are written hundreds
of words later. Today's is grammar rather than position in the issue, which is
why no previous diagnosis reached it, and it is the same shape: a gate written
from one specimen inherits that specimen's syntax.

**The structural cause.** Every gate in that file is written by this seat on the
morning after it found one example. The example supplies the noun, the position
and the grammar all at once, and only the first of the three gets generalised,
because the entry's prose argues about the noun. Nothing in the procedure asks
whether the defect can be restated in a different clause, a different position,
or a different part of speech, and the model's output moves freely across all
three.

**The fix, landed.** The gate now puts its question to every clause, including
the ones hanging off which, that and whose, and names a study, a paper, an
ablation and a claim among the subjects that are not people. Ban list 110. The
generalisation question is added to the canon's pass 4, beside entry 90's sweep,
because a sweep searches the generator for the same words and this asks whether
the same defect has another grammar.

## INC-2026-10-13-a-ban-list-entry-shipped-without-the-sweep-entry-90-requires — two entries were written in one pull request, one was swept over the generator and the other was not, and the unswept one had three supplies (2026-10-13, writer seat)

**Observed by:** the writer seat's run of 2026-10-13, starting from the previous
run's own report that it had swept entry 109.

**What happened.** The run of 2026-10-12 added ban list 108, the weekly that says
today, and ban list 109, the count that is right about how many and wrong about
what they are. Entry 90 of the same register says an entry naming a class is
swept over `prompts/digest.md` in the pull request that adds it, with the count
printed in the review and every hit fixed or justified. Entry 109 was swept and
the sweep found five supplies, four of which were struck. Entry 108 was not
swept, and its review says so without noticing: "Patched as a gate immediately
before the law 15 gate."

Swept today, the tell matched 49 lines of the generator and three of them were
specimens standing where the model writes rather than instructions to it. The
contents-line example opened on "Today, a dense reward that moved terminal
agents fifteen points", in the opening slot, which is exactly where the artifact
printed "Today they are the same conversation" in a weekly. Two absence
specimens ended on "today" where the sentence needs no period word at all. All
three are struck in the pull request of 2026-10-13. The rest sorted cleanly on
the file's own convention, which translates its "this week" to "today" for a
daily and says nothing in the other direction.

**Why this is a repeat.** Entry 90 exists because entry 89 shipped on 2026-10-03
without a sweep and one grep the next morning found three more live in the
generator plus a fourth inside entry 89's own repair. That is occurrence one,
and it was recorded as ban list 90 rather than here, which is itself why this
entry exists: the first occurrence went into the register the rule lives in and
never into the register that reads repeats. This is occurrence two, and the
detail that makes it worth an entry is that the same run swept the other entry
it wrote the same hour, so the rule was being obeyed and applied to one of two.

**The structural cause.** Entry 90's own text says "where a new or existing entry
generalises, run its tell over prompts/digest.md". Whether an entry generalises is
a judgment the writing run makes about its own entry, taken at the end of a long
run, one entry at a time, with no list to tick. Entry 109's tell is a phrase a
grep can hold ("three labs") and entry 108's tell is a word class, so the entry
whose sweep was cheaper got swept. A rule applied per entry by judgment is a rule
that holds for the convenient entry.

**The fix, landed.** The canon's pass 4 now says the sweep is run for every entry
the run adds and the count printed per entry, so an entry with no sweep line is
visible in the review rather than invisible in it. The sweep for 108 is recorded
inside entry 108, where the next reader of that entry will find it.

## INC-2026-10-13-a-retrofit-left-its-own-suites-asserting-cut-sections-and-the-detector-was-never-wired — third of this class, and the first one inside the skill seat's own directory (2026-10-13, skill seat)

**Observed 2026-10-13 by the skill seat, in the weekly run.** Recorded under the
standing rule at the top of this file. This is the same failure shape as
`INC-2026-09-30-the-guard-went-red-and-nobody-read-it` and
`INC-2026-10-06-a-skill-revision-leaves-stale-claim-id-assertions-in-tests`: a
skill revision changes a list, and other files that name members of that list go
stale. Two facts make it worth its own entry rather than a line on the 10-06 one.

**What happened.** `harness-engineering`'s ADR-38 retrofit on 2026-09-30 cut and
renamed every `## ` heading in the file. Nine of the eleven tasks in
`skills/harness-engineering/evals/evals.json` still named the old headings in
their `sections` field, and `skills/harness-engineering/triggers.json`'s
`he-pos-1` still asserted the skill covers multi-agent failure localisation,
which that retrofit cut on measurement. So for thirteen days the gold specimen's
own suites made two false claims about it: that eleven tasks covered its
sections, when four did, and that it answers a question it had stopped
answering. `python3 tools/skill_eval.py --check` printed the first as nine
`failing:` lines the entire time.

**The first new fact: this one is inside this seat's own surface.** The two prior
entries are about `tests/` and `site/`, files the skill seat may not write, and
both concluded that a weekly-revised register needs its readers enumerated in
the revising seat's charter. That conclusion does not reach this case. These two
files live in the skill's own directory, are written by this seat, and were
revised in the same run that renamed the headings. Nothing external was
involved. The lesson has to be stronger: **a retrofit's own directory is the
first place to re-read, not the last.** The 10-06 entry's proposed pre-flight
command (`grep -rn "$(removed_claim_id)" tests/ site/ tools/`) would not have
caught this, because it greps everywhere except `skills/`.

**The second new fact, and the one that matters more: the detector existed and
nothing ran it.** `tools/skill_eval.py --check` has had the heading-comparison
assertion since 2026-10-04, and `skills/_validation/evals/README.md` has
specified it since 2026-09-30, in these words: "every string in `sections` is a
heading of that SKILL.md... Both are decidable with no model." It was right, it
was cheap, and it was never wired. `checks.yml` runs
`tests/test_skill_receipts.py` on changes under `skills/**` and does not run
`tools/skill_eval.py --check` or `skills/_validation/trigger_test.py`. So the
org paid to build a check, documented it as the thing that catches exactly this
defect, and then shipped the defect it was built for. This is a different
failure from the three stale-assertion entries, which are all about a check that
went red and was not read. Here nothing ever went red.

**Fix.**

1. *Shipped here.* Every `sections` entry in `harness-engineering`'s suite now
   names a heading that exists. Four tasks remap onto the three deltas; five are
   reclassified as controls carrying an `excluded_reason`, because the sections
   they measured no longer exist and ADR-38 rule 5 keeps such a task as a
   control rather than deleting it. `he-pos-1` is rewritten against delta 3,
   which had no positive case, and its old prompt is kept as `he-conf-2` so the
   cut stays on the record.
2. *The real fix, filed and not shipped, because `.github/` is not this seat's
   surface.* Both checks belong in `checks.yml`'s `skills/**` path filter, the
   eval conformance check as a hard failure and the trigger suite as a reported
   number. Ledger entry dated 2026-10-13 in `docs/ideas.md`. This is the fix
   that counts, and company standard **L-A22** is why: "the gate goes in the
   command, not in the charter", because a rule enforced by charter text is
   enforced at the reliability of a model reading a file. **L-A16** names the
   same gap from the other side, "configured is not in effect": the check was
   built and documented, and nothing proves a capability is live until a run
   log shows it served a real turn. A built check that no workflow calls is the
   purest case of that rule this register holds.
3. *The weaker fix, stated for completeness and explicitly second.* A charter
   line in `prompts/skill-agent.md`, which is not this seat's surface either:
   after any revision that renames or removes a `## ` heading, run `python3
   tools/skill_eval.py --check` and `python3
   skills/_validation/trigger_test.py` before the commit, and treat a
   `failing:` line naming your own slug as a blocker. Worth having, and by
   L-A22 it is not the answer. If only one of items 2 and 3 ever lands, it
   should be item 2.

**What the org should take from it.** Three entries in this register now say a
weekly-revised list went stale in a file that names its members. The new one
says something the other two cannot: we already built the check. The gap between
"a check exists" and "a check runs" is where this defect lived for thirteen
days, and it is the same gap `INC-2026-10-12-meta-review-proposal-merged-never-
deployed` describes for a merged self-improvement that never deployed. Recording
a rule and enforcing it are two gates, which is the lesson the charter's own
"Check the register before you ship" section already teaches, and this is that
lesson applied to a tool rather than to a register.

## INC-2026-10-14-the-first-dispatch-that-ran-died-at-a-bot-gate-no-workflow-configures — the `dispatch-403` saga's next link: the call finally created a run, and the run refused itself (2026-10-14, frontend seat, observed by the PM seat)

**Observed 2026-10-14, triaged under `docs/standards/pm.md` §11.7** (the
PM's failed-run triage, run by a message-triggered pass). `gh run list
--status failure` surfaced exactly one failure in the window: frontend-agent,
run [38594124029](https://github.com/alexandrapaiz/alexandria/actions/runs/38594124029),
`workflow_dispatch`, failed in 63 seconds with zero commits, zero branch,
zero PR (the no-ship tripwire caught that cleanly and correctly).

**Why this is not another `dispatch-403`, even though it is the same saga.**
`INC-2026-09-24-dispatch-403`, `INC-2026-09-26-dispatch-403-repeat` and
`INC-2026-09-29-dispatch-403-repeat` all document the same prior failure: a
PM `gh workflow run` call never created a run at all (`HTTP 403: Resource
not accessible by integration`). This run is the opposite shape. `gh api
repos/alexandrapaiz/alexandria/actions/runs/38594124029 --jq
'.triggering_actor.login'` returns `github-actions[bot]`, and `gh run list
--event workflow_dispatch --limit 20` shows no other `workflow_dispatch`
event anywhere in the repo between 2026-10-05 and this one. As far as this
register can tell from the outside, **this is the first `workflow_dispatch`
call in this repo's history that got past the 403 and actually created a
run**, which the three entries above could never confirm because none of
them got this far.

**And the run it created died anyway, one step later, for a new reason.**
`gh run view 38594124029 --log` shows the `anthropics/claude-code-action@v1`
step itself refusing to execute:

    ##[error]Action failed with error: Workflow initiated by non-human
    actor: github-actions (type: Bot). Add bot to allowed_bots list or
    use '*' to allow all bots.

Exit code 1, 4 seconds into the step. The action has its own gate on who is
allowed to have triggered the workflow that calls it, and a `workflow_dispatch`
fired by `GITHUB_TOKEN` from inside another seat's run — exactly the
mechanism ADR-033 (charter §5) grants and names, "a parent run started a
child run with the runner's own token" — presents to GitHub as the generic
`github-actions[bot]` actor, not a human. `grep -L allowed_bots
.github/workflows/agent-*.yml` returns all twelve workflow files: none of
them configure the allow-list, so this gate is not tuned against frontend
specifically, it is simply unconfigured everywhere.

**Classified under §11.7: Configuration, not a real defect in the frontend
seat's own code or charter**, and not transient (the same input fails the
same way every time until a workflow file changes). No rerun. Per §11.7's
own routing for this class and per `docs/standards/pm.md` §15's "who owns
what" ("a product seat does not edit `.github/workflows` in its own repo"),
this is filed here and handed off on the board to
`alexandra-systems/exo-centralizer` rather than fixed in place; this seat's
boundaries also forbid touching workflow files directly.

**The scope is every seat, not frontend.** Nothing about this gate is
frontend-specific. Any `workflow_dispatch` that any seat fires against any
other seat's workflow, through the exact mechanism charter §5 and ADR-033
grant, will reach this same gate and die the same way, because the fired
run always presents as `github-actions[bot]` and no workflow file allows
it. **Until a workflow file adds `allowed_bots: '*'` (or the specific bot
login) to every `agent-*.yml`'s `claude-code-action` step, charter §5's
dispatch authority is a call that can now reach GitHub but still cannot
produce a working run on the other end** — which is a different failure
mode than the 403 saga, not a fix for it. The two gates happened to be
stacked, so clearing the first one (whatever changed between 2026-09-29 and
today) only now exposed the second.

**What did not happen.** The board item this run was dispatched for
(`03029cad`, "Ship the Left-Behind Index as a public page") stayed in
`Backlog`: the run died before its first tool call, so it never reached the
"move to In progress" instruction in its own prompt. Nothing to revert
there. A comment was added to that item naming this run's specific failure,
distinct from the 403 comment already on it from 2026-10-13.

**Handoff filed on the board** to `alexandra-systems/exo-centralizer`,
citing this entry and the run URL, asking for `allowed_bots` on the
`agent-*.yml` workflow files. Not fired as a dispatch and not reworked by
this seat, because workflow files are HQ's surface per §15, and because
the fix is not diagnosable as a rerun candidate.

## INC-2026-10-14-dispatch-403-half-fixed — the ambient token was never the one `permissions:` governs, and fixing it exposed a second gate (2026-10-14, PM seat; renumbered by the engineer seat)

**Renumbered, not rewritten (engineer seat, 2026-10-14, second run).** This
entry was filed as a second `INC-2026-09-24-dispatch-403`, which is the id of
the entry it amends at line 3805 of this file. `tools/check_registers.py`
calls that merge damage and blocks on it, so `python3
tools/check_registers.py` exited 1 on `main` and
`tests/test_check_registers.py::test_this_repository_has_no_merge_damage_in_its_registers`
failed with it. The id is now dated the day this was observed, which is what
the numbering rule at the top of this file asks for, and **the old id is
recorded here rather than dropped, because that rule says never to renumber
silently.** Nothing else about the entry is changed, and no reference
elsewhere in the repository pointed at the duplicate: all fourteen mentions of
`INC-2026-09-24-dispatch-403` outside this file mean the original. Its own
finding, below, is the PM seat's and stands as written.

**Twenty days open, found working today.** `INC-2026-09-24-dispatch-403`
(above) left a standing question for the ExO or engineer: whether
`github.token` inside a `claude-code-action` step is the same value the
job's `permissions: actions: write` block actually governs. It is not.
`docs/standards/pm.md` §11.5 (vendored into this repo 2026-10-12, after
the incident was filed) answers it directly: the Claude Code action
exchanges the run's OIDC token for its own GitHub App installation
token and overwrites `GH_TOKEN`/`GITHUB_TOKEN` with it, scopes fixed by
the action's own defaults rather than by the workflow's `permissions:`
block. The job's real `${{ github.token }}` survives under a different
name, `DEFAULT_WORKFLOW_TOKEN`, and that is the one the `permissions:`
block governs.

This run confirmed both halves hold here, not only in prose: `GH_TOKEN`
and `DEFAULT_WORKFLOW_TOKEN` are two different token values in this
job's own environment (confirmed by direct comparison, prefixes
`ghs_123670…` versus `ghs_15368…`), and
`GH_TOKEN="$DEFAULT_WORKFLOW_TOKEN" gh workflow run agent-frontend.yml
-f owner_instructions='…'` returned a run URL
(https://github.com/alexandrapaiz/alexandria/actions/runs/38594124029,
confirmed `in_progress`) where the bare `gh workflow run` call eighteen
runs in a row had 403'd. HQ's `tools/gh-actions.sh` wrapper, which
would have made this the default rather than a one-off, is not vendored
into this repo; until it is, every dispatch call here needs the same
`GH_TOKEN="$DEFAULT_WORKFLOW_TOKEN"` prefix by hand. Filed to
`docs/ideas.md`, handed off to the exo centralizer rather than the
engineer, since `.github/workflows/` is HQ's surface in every product
repo (standard §15) and not this seat's or the frontend seat's to edit.

**The run that proved the fix also found what was hiding behind it.**
The dispatch created a real run (38594124029, `frontend-agent`) for the
first time in eighteen days, and that run failed in 4 seconds, before
the model read a single token of its prompt:

```
Action failed with error: Workflow initiated by non-human actor:
github-actions (type: Bot). Add bot to allowed_bots list or use '*'
to allow all bots.
```

`claude-code-action` has its own actor-type gate, separate from the
GitHub permissions model this incident is about: it refuses to run when
the triggering actor is a bot unless the workflow's `allowed_bots` input
names it. A dispatch made with `DEFAULT_WORKFLOW_TOKEN` is attributed to
`github-actions[bot]`, not to a human and not to the `claude[bot]` app
installation a normal PR event carries, so it trips this gate every
time. This is a second, previously invisible blocker: the 403 masked it
completely, because no run had ever reached the action's own actor check
before today. Classified **configuration** per `docs/standards/pm.md`
§11.7 — a workflow file, not a seat's code — and `.github/workflows/` is
HQ's surface per standard §15, not this seat's or the frontend seat's to
edit. Handed off to `alexandra-systems/exo-centralizer` on the board
(message posted this run) rather than fixed here: every `agent-*.yml`
that the PM might ever dispatch needs `allowed_bots: '*'` (or
`github-actions`, named) on its `claude-code-action` step, or the first
half of this fix is dead code that only ever produces this second error.
No rerun; the same actor fails the same way every time until the
workflow changes.

## INC-2026-10-14-the-two-apps-the-drift-guard-could-not-see — "never recorded" read as unmeasured for five days, so three merged fixes never reached the stage they repair and the press printed nothing twice (2026-10-14, engineer seat)

**Observed by:** the engineer seat's scheduled run of 2026-10-14, reading the
public receipt at 01:49 UTC as the first step of its own observation.

**What was wrong.** `tools/delivery_health.py`'s deploy surface had three
states for an app and used two of them. An app with a recorded digest matching
the trunk was `ok`. One with a stale digest was drift, dated and alarmed. One
with no row at all was `unknown (never recorded)`, on the reasoning that
dating an unmeasured app from its last commit would cry wolf. That reasoning
is right about the number and wrong about the state, and the distinction it
missed is one line of code wide: an app whose module calls `record_runtime`
writes its row on the first run of any deploy built from that commit, so no
row means the running image predates that commit. The age of the commit is a
lower bound on the age of the image. It is drift, and it is datable.

**The sequence, with the dates, because the shape is only visible in order.**

| when | what |
|---|---|
| 2026-10-07 15:15 UTC | the last claim distill ever wrote |
| 2026-10-08 | the primary provider stops answering, and distill's fallback path, paced for a day it does not have, produces nothing |
| 2026-10-09 18:02 | `807d403` adds `distill` and `ingest` to the guard and asks them to record. Its own incident entry says plainly that both read `unknown` until the owner runs `modal deploy` |
| 2026-10-11 16:47 | `e289242`, the fallback paced by the minute it actually has |
| 2026-10-12 02:22 | `c005e9e` and `66f7e87`, the fallback's day shared three ways |
| 2026-10-12 09:00 | the Monday press cron fires and has no new claims to print |
| 2026-10-13 | launch day. Still `2026-W40` on the site, created 2026-10-05 |
| 2026-10-14 01:49 | the receipt: `claims_newest` 2026-10-07, `distill_pending` 2,223, and a `deploy` block listing three apps where the guard watches five |

Every fix to the thing that was broken landed inside the window where the one
surface that grades deploys was saying `unknown` about the broken stage.

**And it was quieter than `unknown`, which is the detail worth keeping.** The
unknowns were reported only when nothing else alarmed. The old `judge_deploy`
returned on its `alarms` branch before it reached them, so measured against
the live rows and the real history, the surface read `failing` with the
headline "triage is 1.2 days behind" and said nothing whatsoever about the two
apps that had never recorded. The `unknown` that three seats saw and wrote
down was the quiet day. The loud day was louder about the wrong app. Both
readings leave a reader with no instruction to deploy `distill`, and the new
code names the never-recorded apps in the same headline as the drifted ones.

**The cost.** Two issues. The product's only output missed its Monday and then
missed launch day, and `claims` has not moved in seven days while 2,223 papers
wait. `INC-2026-10-12-the-press-had-no-degraded-path-and-the-week-got-no-issue`
is the same morning read from the press's end, and this is the cause at the
other end of it.

**Why it is recorded as a repeat.** Fifth sighting of one shape, which is that
a merge is not a deploy and nothing in this repository closes that gap on its
own: incident 24, PR #110 (merged 2026-09-26, inert for days, three documents
calling it live), `INC-2026-10-10-four-editorial-grades-named-the-merge-as-the-
gate-when-the-gate-is-the-deploy`, and
`INC-2026-10-12-meta-review-proposal-merged-never-deployed`.

It is also the second half of
`INC-2026-10-09-the-drift-guard-watched-three-of-five-scheduled-jobs`, and
that is the part worth reading twice. That entry closes with a section titled
"The part that is still open", which says both new apps read `unknown` until
somebody runs two commands. It was correct, it was specific, it named the
commands, and it was filed by the right seat in the right register. Then five
days passed, because `unknown` is not a state anything escalates. **A pending
action parked in a non-escalating state is indistinguishable from a pending
action nobody took.** The research seat met the same `unknown` on 2026-10-12
and read it the same way, as a limitation of the instrument rather than as the
alarm it was.

**It is also both halves of L-A21, in one surface.** That standard says a
gate is judged by what it can see, and that a gate which saw nothing is a
failure rather than a quiet pass. The deploy surface had the first half: its
answer about the three apps it could see was correct the whole time, which is
what made it sound healthy. And it had the second half in the strongest
available form, because `unknown (never recorded)` is the literal rendering of
"this gate saw nothing", and it was being read as a quiet pass by every seat
that met it, including the two that wrote it down. The test to run on a gate,
by L-A21's own words, is to name a change that would break what it governs and
ask whether the gate would have seen it. The change was a merge that is not
deployed. The gate's whole job is that change. It could not see it for the two
apps where it was true.

And it is L-A9's shape once more, recording is not enforcing, with a new
detail: the test that asserted the wrong reading
(`test_an_app_that_never_recorded_is_unmeasured_while_the_others_are_judged`)
was defined below its own file's `__main__` block, so `main()`'s walk over
`globals()` never reached it and `python3 tests/test_deploy_drift.py` printed
"all checks passed" without running it. Four tests in two files were in that
position, in two files that `test_ci_coverage.py` pins as run by no workflow
at all, which means a direct run was the only run they were ever going to get.
A wrong assertion nothing executes and a right assertion nothing executes are
the same artifact.

**What was built this run.** `recording_asked_at` dates the commit that asks
an app for a row, by pickaxe over the app's own module at the trunk.
`undeployed_since` names the commits an image older than that commit cannot
contain, since the usual recovery-by-replay has no reported digest to replay
against. An app that has never recorded while its code asks it to is now
`failing` with the deploy command in its evidence. An app whose code does not
ask is still `unknown`, which keeps the cry-wolf case the old reasoning was
right about. An app added within the grace window is still a pending deploy. The mail is withheld for these, with the reason in the evidence,
because the alarm's cooldown is a column on the row they do not have. The
runner block in both affected test files moved to the end of the file, and
`test_ci_coverage.py` now fails if any test file strands a test below its
`__main__` block.

**What is still open and belongs to the owner.** The guard can only say it.
`grep -rln "modal deploy" .github/workflows/` still returns nothing, so no
merged change to `pipeline/` has ever reached production without somebody
remembering a command. `.github/workflows-pending/modal-deploy.yml` has been
written and waiting since 2026-10-08, and it needs `MODAL_TOKEN_ID` and
`MODAL_TOKEN_SECRET` plus a `git mv`. Six days of rent on that item bought the
two missing issues above. Until it is applied, the two commands are
`modal deploy pipeline/distill.py` and `modal deploy pipeline/ingest.py`.

## INC-2026-10-14-the-fix-to-the-guard-that-watches-deploys-fired-no-merge-check — the path filter's fourth sighting, on the pull request repairing the surface the press depends on (2026-10-14, engineer seat)

**Observed by:** the engineer seat's scheduled run of 2026-10-14, running the
charter's pre-ship gate against its own pull request, exactly as
`INC-2026-10-10-a-whole-pull-request-fired-no-merge-check` was observed four
days earlier.

```
$ gh pr checks 292
no checks reported on the 'engineer/2026-10-14-distill-dark' branch
```

**What it is.** Today's diff is `tools/delivery_health.py`, three files under
`tests/`, and three documents. `.github/workflows/checks.yml`'s `paths` list
names `tools/board.py`, `tools/run_report.py` and `tools/graph_audit.py`, and
fourteen individual test files, and none of today's. So the pull request that
repairs the deploy guard, and the four new tests that hold its boundaries, are
asserted on this branch and silent on the merge.

**Why it is recorded as its own entry rather than a line on the 2026-10-10
one.** Because the number is the finding. That entry's title says "third
distinct failure" and its own text says the staged replacement's rent was
three days. The rent is now six, the sighting is the fourth, and the two
measurements this run made of the same filter are worth reading together: the
diff fires no check, and the file holding the test this run had to rewrite is
in `test_ci_coverage.py`'s uncovered pin, so the only run those tests were
ever going to get was a seat typing a command. A gate that depends on a seat
remembering is the thing every entry on this page is about.

**What would close it** is unchanged and is not this seat's to apply: item 17
in `docs/agents/pending-workflow-changes.md`, staged and verified in
`.github/workflows-pending/checks.yml` since 2026-10-07, which replaces the
filename list with a run of the whole suite.

**Fifth sighting, same day, same branch, and narrower than it first looked
(engineer seat, second run).** The pull request that supersedes this one, #294,
carries every file above plus `tools/press_watch.py`, `tests/test_press_watch.py`
and a new workflow in the pending lane. For its first eight commits
`gh pr checks 294` answered `no checks reported`, and the API agreed:
`actions/runs?branch=engineer/2026-10-14-quiet-send-guardrail` returned
`total_count: 0` at 16:10, 16:14 and 16:16 UTC, after two pushes that changed
`tools/board.py`, which is in that filter's own `paths` list. The ninth push,
a merge of `main`, created a `pull_request` run at 16:17.

So the honest version of this sighting is not that the branch fires nothing.
It is that the branch fires a check which says nothing about the branch's own
work. The job starts only because this run also edited `tools/board.py`, and
what it runs is the press budget plus `tests/test_board.py`. The 46 tests in
`tests/test_press_watch.py` that hold the quiet-send guardrail are outside the
filter, as is the tool itself, so the green tick on this pull request is
evidence about a file this run touched by accident rather than about the file
it was written to add.

Why two pushes that matched the filter produced no run is not something this
run could establish from inside a sandbox, and it is written here as an
observation rather than a mechanism. The part that needs no explanation is
unchanged: item 17 of `docs/agents/pending-workflow-changes.md` has been
staged and verified since 2026-10-07, which is seven days, and it replaces the

2026-10-05T09:01:04Z.

own first run of today named one register over, in

action parked in a state that nothing escalates is indistinguishable from a

artifacts that are supposed to be loud. A card in Backlog, a sprint item with

- 2026-10-14, second run: this entry.

## INC-2026-10-14-the-register-gate-was-blocking-on-main-and-nothing-ran-it-before-the-merge — two entries shared one id for the fifth time, and the tool that forbids it is pinned out of CI (2026-10-14, engineer seat, second run)

**Observed by:** the engineer seat's second run of 2026-10-14, 16:21 UTC,
running `python3 -m pytest tests/ -q` after merging `origin/main` at `365bc79`
into its own branch. The suite came back `1 failed, 1422 passed` and the
failure was `tests/test_check_registers.py::test_this_repository_has_no_merge_damage_in_its_registers`:

    docs/agents/incidents.md:12885: incident id INC-2026-09-24-dispatch-403
    already used at line 3805

`python3 tools/check_registers.py` on `main` exits 1 with the same line, under
its own headline, "the registers are damaged and every seat reads them".

**What happened.** A correct and useful entry, the PM seat's finding that the
dispatch 403 is half fixed, was filed on 2026-10-14 under the id of the entry
it amends. The numbering rule at the top of this file asks for
`INC-YYYY-MM-DD-slug` dated the day the incident was observed, and an
amendment to an older entry is still a new entry with its own date. Nothing
about the finding is wrong. The id is.

**The repeat, which is why this is filed, and it is two classes at once.**

Two entries sharing one id is the collision the date scheme replaced the
counter to end. The header of this file says the allocator "has now happened
four times". This is the fifth, and it is the first one that is not an
accident of two branches: it is one seat deliberately reusing a slug to say
"this is about that", which is a real need the scheme has no spelling for.

The second class is incident 20's, which every charter's "Check the register
before you ship" step exists to close: **a gate that exists, is correct, and
runs nowhere between the writing and the merge.** `tools/check_registers.py`
had this finding available the whole time. It is `blocking` rather than a
warning, by its own design, precisely so this cannot merge. It ran in no
workflow, because `tests/test_check_registers.py` is pinned in
`tests/test_ci_coverage.py`'s `UNCOVERED` set, and `checks.yml` stayed green
on `main` through the merge because that file is not in its fourteen steps.
So the register gate and the merge check were both working and neither was
pointed at the other.

**What this run did about it.** Renumbered the newer entry to
`INC-2026-10-14-dispatch-403-half-fixed`, with the old id recorded inside it,
because the rule at the top of this file says never to renumber silently. The
PM's text is otherwise untouched: the finding is that seat's and it is right.
Checked every reference first, and all fourteen mentions of
`INC-2026-09-24-dispatch-403` elsewhere in the repository mean the original
entry, so nothing pointed at the duplicate. `python3 tools/check_registers.py`
now exits 0 and the suite is green on this branch.

**What would close the class rather than this instance.** Item 17 of
`docs/agents/pending-workflow-changes.md`, seven days staged, which replaces
`checks.yml`'s filename list with a run of the whole suite. That is the change
that makes this gate fire on the pull request that breaks it, which is the
only version of this fix that does not depend on a seat remembering to run a
command. Measured today: `python3 tools/ci_coverage.py --only
.github/workflows-pending/checks.yml` is `53 of 53`.
## INC-2026-10-14-the-standup-ran-205-turns-and-shipped-nothing — a scheduled PM pass finished clean and left no commit, no branch, no pull request (2026-10-14, PM seat)

**What happened.** The 2026-10-14 15:46:59 UTC scheduled standup (run
`38592352927`) ran the model step to completion: `is_error: false`,
`num_turns: 205` against a 300-turn cap (68%, under the cap-ratio line),
`$9.93` spent, zero permission denials. The no-ship tripwire then failed
the job: no commit ahead of `main`, no seat branch pushed, no pull
request of any kind, and no uncommitted diff in the sandbox either. The
run did not merely lose work at teardown (incident 3's shape); it never
produced any in the first place, despite 205 turns and over half an hour
of wall time.

**Why this is a new class, not a repeat.** Every prior no-ship entry in
this file involves either a crash before the first push or uncommitted
work lost at teardown. This run crashed nowhere and had nothing dirty to
lose: it read for 205 turns and never once wrote. The charter's own
"ship first" rule exists exactly to prevent this (open the draft PR in
the first few turns, before substantial thinking), and this run did not
follow it — not even the fallback case ("if the run genuinely produces
nothing worth shipping, say that in a draft PR and close it") which
still requires opening something.

**The likely contributing cause, named rather than guessed as certain.**
`docs/sprints/pending.md` is approximately 1,970 lines and growing by a
full dated section almost every run; `docs/standards/pm.md` and this
seat's own charter are each several hundred lines on top of that. A
standup that reads its full required context before acting spends a
large, and growing, fraction of its turn budget on reading alone. This
run's 205 turns and $9.93 cost are the most expensive clean standup in
the visible run history; the next one may cap out reading before it
writes anything, the same failure this incident already shows in a
softer form.

**Not fixed this run.** No rerun (the input was a scheduled trigger, not
a transient fault, and the same context would reproduce the same risk).
Proposed rather than done: `docs/sprints/pending.md` should get a
dated-archive split (old entries moved out of the file the standup must
read each time) so the standup's own history stops being the thing that
starves it. That is a ceremony-sized change, not a standup-sized one;
named here for the next Monday ceremony (2026-10-19) or the ExO.
## INC-2026-10-14-two-generator-gates-asked-for-a-reading-and-never-failed — one gate said count and named no unit, one gate said no two alike and counted nothing, and ten grades read past both (2026-10-14, writer seat)

**What happened.** The tenth grade of 2026-W40 found two defects in plain
arithmetic, both forbidden by hard gates that were in the deployed file on the
day the issue printed.

The new-work slot opened "Three papers this week test what happens when you
push the agent stack in directions no benchmark yet covers" and put four items
under it. The gate against that calls itself "arithmetic rather than judgment",
says to count what appears under the sentence, and never says what to count.
Its four examples are all nouns for the issue's own contents rather than units
a reader can see, so the writer picks the unit, and a writer who picks the unit
can always rescue the count. The fourth item there names no paper, which is how
this one was rescued.

The issue carried eight evidence grades standing on three frames. Four opened
on the identical three words. Two more were the same frame as each other about
the same paper, one in the body and one in the reading list. The gate against
that says "No two grades in the issue begin the same way, none begins on the
word 'evidence', and no two are built on the same frame", and asks for no count
at all. The step it does ask for is a judgment the writer makes about its own
prose.

**Why it is a repeat and not a discovery.** The class is already written down
twice in this seat's own registers, in both directions, and neither recording
reached the generator's gates.

`docs/voice/canon.md` has said since 2026-09-29 that a law asserting coverage
is graded by a count and never by a reading, and since 2026-10-13 that whether
something generalises is "a judgment a tired run makes about its own prose".
Both sentences were written about the grade's verdicts. Neither was ever turned
on the generator's gates, which are the same instrument pointed the other way,
and every gate in that file which holds was converted to a count after a print
walked past it.

**The sharper half, and it is about where the evidence was sitting.** Both
defects were quoted verbatim in this seat's own earlier reviews of the same
artifact, in blocks pasted as evidence for a different law.
`docs/voice/reviews/2026-10-06.md` quotes "Three papers this week test what
happens when you push [...]" inside a list of standalone lines, while counting
shapes. `docs/voice/reviews/2026-10-05.md` prints all four "The authors' own"
grades in a numbered block, while finding that grades sat in the position the
meaning line needed. Each run quoted the string, graded the one law it had come
for, and moved on. Nine and eight grades followed, each re-reading the reviews
and never re-reading the quotations in them.

Canon pass 5's fifth question already covers the half-graded SENTENCE and the
sixth covers the forgiven half of a VERDICT. Neither covers a block of the
artifact quoted inside a review, which is a third place a half-read thing can
hide, and the cheapest one to check because the text is already extracted and
sitting in the file.

**The fix.** Both gates are patched in the writer pull request of 2026-10-14,
each as a count rather than a reading, and five supplied specimens are struck
from the two composition rules that were handing the shapes over. Ban list 112
and 113 carry the entries and the sweeps. The grading procedure gains a step
that puts the remaining laws to every block a review quotes, which is the only
part of this that would have found either defect nine days earlier.

**What it says about the seat.** This is not a reading failure that more care
fixes. Ten careful grades read past both, which is the evidence that the
procedure and not the attention was short. The pattern across all of it is one
sentence: an instruction that asks somebody to look is satisfied by looking,
and only an instruction that asks for a number can come back wrong.
## INC-2026-10-14-the-sticky-nav-ghost-is-re-investigated-every-run — third run to spend turns on a 1 to 3 percent bleed-through that measurement has already settled twice (2026-10-14, frontend seat)

**What happened.** The weekly visual run scrolled the desk page on a phone
viewport, magnified the top of the frame to three times scale, and read the
scrolled content showing through the sticky nav as a legibility collision
between two layers of text. The run was about to file it. Measuring it with
`docs/design/harness/ink.mjs` instead returned 252 of 255 for the darkest
pixel in the empty space of the bar at 390, and 247 of 255 at 1440, which is a
ghost of one to three percent and not a finding.

**Why it is an incident rather than a near miss.** The harness README already
records this: "Twice now a run has nearly filed the sticky nav as transparent;
measured, the ink behind it is 247 to 255 of 255, which is a ghost at about
3%." This run is the third. The standing rule at the top of this file is that
an issue occurring more than once is recorded at the moment it repeats, with
no judgment call, and a repeat that goes unrecorded is itself an incident.

**The cause, which is not the nav.** The nav is correct. `rgba(255,255,255,0.94)`
over a 22px backdrop blur is a deliberate value that a previous run raised from
0.85 for this exact reason, and the comment in the stylesheet says so. What
repeats is the method. A run looks at a screenshot, magnifies a region to read
it, and the magnification is what makes a 3 percent ghost legible. The enlarged
crop is evidence that something is there and is not evidence of how strong it
is, because enlarging does not preserve the impression of contrast that the eye
would get at one to one.

**The fix applied this run.** The harness README's bullet on `ink.mjs` now says
in its own words that the sticky nav question is settled, gives the two numbers,
and tells the next run to measure before filing rather than after. Prose that
records a conclusion is weaker than prose that names the next action, which is
why the bullet changed rather than the count in it.

**What would close this class.** A check in the harness that reads the bar's
empty space and prints the number every run, so the answer arrives before the
question does. That is a harness change rather than a site change and it is on
the board for this seat.
## INC-2026-09-20-the-arxiv-406-is-rate-limiting-wearing-the-wrong-status-code — the same 406 diagnosed three times and never once retried (observed 2026-09-20, filed 2026-10-14, engineer seat)

Recorded under the standing rule: this failure has now happened three
times and each time it was patched with a different theory of its cause.

**What happened.** `tools/check_issue_citations.py` is the accuracy half
of the pre-send quality tier: it is the only thing that checks a cited
title against the paper its link resolves to. Run against 2026-W37 this
morning it died on `HTTP Error 406: Not Acceptable` and exited 1.

The file already carried two comments about 406s, both written by earlier
runs that hit the same error and guessed at a header:

- "the commas in id_list must stay literal; arxiv answers 406 to %2C"
- "arxiv answers 406 to urllib's default Accept header"

This run started on a third guess, that arXiv had begun refusing
`Accept: application/atom+xml`, and the evidence looked good: curl
returned 200 to nine consecutive requests while urllib returned 406 to
all of them. Then the same test, run twice more, returned 200 to every
urllib variant including the ones that had just failed, and 406 to a
single-id request that had succeeded a minute earlier. The 406 is
time-varying. It is rate limiting wearing the wrong status code, and no
header change ever fixed it. Two of the three comments in that file are
probably wrong for the same reason.

**Why it kept happening.** Each encounter was a one-off run under time
pressure, and a header change that is followed by a success looks like a
fix. Nothing in the tool distinguished "this request is malformed" from
"this service is refusing me right now", so every failure presented as
the former. The 406 status is a real contributor here: a 429 would have
been diagnosed correctly in thirty seconds by all three runs.

**The fix.** Retry with backoff (15s, 45s, 120s) on 406, 429 and 5xx,
with the reasoning written where the next person will read it. Afterwards
the checker ran clean against 2026-W37: 9 citations checked, 0 failed. It
runs once a day, so three and a half minutes of patience costs nothing.

**What the org should take from it.** A retry is the first response to an
intermittent external failure, not the third. Before changing a request
to fix an error, run the unchanged request again. This tool is not the
only one that talks to a free API on someone else's terms:
`pipeline/weekly.py`'s citation slow loop calls Semantic Scholar and
`pipeline/ingest.py` calls arXiv, and both should be read against this
entry the next time either misbehaves.

**Filed late, and the delay is part of the record.** This entry was
written on 2026-09-20 on the branch that carries the fix, and that branch
stayed open for twenty-four days, so the register never held it. It is
being filed now by the run that cleared the branch's conflict. An
incident that exists only on an unmerged branch is an incident the org
does not have, which is the same lesson L-E10 teaches about code: `main`
is the one place where work that is built but unmerged is invisible.

**It also arrived carrying the wrong id.** The original took the number
23, with a note reasoning about which sequential number was free. Main
issued 23 to a different event five days later, and the collision was
invisible until this merge. That is incident 29's class and it is
recorded again today as
`INC-2026-10-14-an-open-branch-held-two-ids-main-had-since-issued`.

## INC-2026-10-14-an-open-branch-held-two-ids-main-had-since-issued — the sequential allocator collides across time, and only a merge conflict reveals it (2026-10-14, engineer seat)

Recorded under the standing rule. This is incident 29's class, which is a
sequential id allocated on a branch by a run that cannot see the whole
register, and it has now happened again with a detail incident 29 does not
cover: the collision was latent for twenty-four days.

**What happened.** The pre-send quality gate's branch was opened on
2026-09-20 and stayed open. On it, two ids were allocated by reading the
highest number then visible: incident 23, for the arXiv 406 entry, and
ADR-28, named in `pipeline/weekly.py`'s docstring for the gate itself. In
the twenty-four days that followed, main issued incident 23 to the Kimi
routing rollout and ADR-28 to the writer seat. Neither collision was
detectable from the branch, because both numbers were free when they were
taken and nothing on the branch changes when main issues one.

**Why the existing fix did not catch it.** Incident 29's remedy is the
date-scoped id, `INC-YYYY-MM-DD-slug`, and it works: a date-scoped id
cannot collide. What it does not do is reach a branch that was written
before the remedy, or an ADR, which still carries a sequential number by
its own convention. So the remedy holds for new entries written by runs
that have read the rule, and the exposure is every long-open branch that
predates it plus every ADR number ever reserved on a branch.

**The repair in this run.** The 406 entry is filed under
`INC-2026-09-20-the-arxiv-406-is-rate-limiting-wearing-the-wrong-status-code`,
with its observation date kept and its filing date named. The docstring's
ADR-28 reference is now a reference to the decision that actually carded
this work, which is the writer seat's ADR-28, and that is the right
citation rather than a repaired wrong one: ADR-28 is where the owner
deferred the pre-send gate and carded it to this seat.

**What the org should take from it.** A merge conflict in a register file
is not only a text conflict. It is the only detector the org has for an id
that two branches both believe they own, and resolving one by taking
either side wholesale destroys the evidence. `.github/workflows-pending/`
holds an `adr-numbers.yml` that would catch the ADR half on a pull
request. It is one of the staged workflows no seat can apply, which is the
sixth day this register has recorded a staged fix nobody holds the
permission to install.

**Second finding from the same cause, recorded here rather than
separately.** The branch was 1,239 commits behind main when it was
reopened. In that time the press was rebuilt around a weekly-only cadence
on a different provider, which is the exact assumption the branch's other
half contradicts, so clearing the conflict meant deciding a product
question rather than resolving text. A branch does not merely go stale. It
goes wrong, and the longer it stays open the more of its own reasoning it
loses the right to assert.

## INC-2026-10-15-the-register-gates-fix-sat-in-an-unmerged-pr-while-main-stayed-red (security seat, run 9)

**Filed as a repeat, and the half that is new is the second day.** The debug
and security charter asks one question that is about the present rather than
the past, which is whether the guard covering a change is green right now.
It was not. `python3 -m pytest tests/ -q` on `main` at c1ddd58 is
`1 failed, 1404 passed`, and the single failure is
`test_check_registers.py::test_this_repository_has_no_merge_damage_in_its_registers`
reporting that two entries in this file share the id
`INC-2026-09-24-dispatch-403`.

**The duplicate itself is already filed and is not what this entry adds.**
The engineer seat found it on 2026-10-14, wrote
`INC-2026-10-14-the-register-gate-was-blocking-on-main-and-nothing-ran-it-before-the-merge`
for the pre-merge half, and fixed it in commit 98d670b by dating the newer
entry and recording the old id inside it, which is what the numbering rule at
the top of this file asks for. That work is correct and this seat did not
redo it.

**What is new is where that fix is.** It is not on `main`. Commit 98d670b
lives on `engineer/2026-10-14-quiet-send-guardrail`, whose pull request #294
was closed as superseded, and it was carried forward to
`engineer/2026-10-15-undeployed-pipeline`, which is open as #301. So the
breakage merged and the fix did not. The duplicate landed on `main` at
16:13 on 2026-10-14 by way of #295, and it was still there 25 hours later
when this run measured it. For that whole period the repository's own
answer to "are the registers intact" was no, the incident entry recording
that was also unmerged and therefore unreadable by anyone working from
`main`, and every seat that read `main` saw a clean register and a red suite
with no explanation in the register.

**Why this is a repeat and not a new class.**
`INC-2026-09-30-the-guard-went-red-and-nobody-read-it` is the same shape, and
the clause it added to `docs/agents/runtime-changes.md` is the clause that
caught this. That clause says a `failure` is a finding before you have read a
single commit, and it says the auditor owns reporting it even when fixing it
belongs to another seat. It does not say what to do when the fix already
exists and is waiting on a merge, which is this case and is the gap worth
naming. A fix in an open pull request protects nobody. Measured against the
state of `main`, an unmerged fix and no fix are the same fix.

**This seat deliberately did not fix it a second time.** Renaming the heading
here would put the same rename in two branches at one anchor, which is
incident 6 exactly, and #301 also inserts 71 lines immediately below that
heading. So the correct action was to leave the rename to #301, report the red
state, and append this entry at the end of the file where it cannot collide.
The owner's action is to merge #301, after which the suite goes green with no
further edit. This entry costs nothing if that merge happens today and is the
only record of the window if it does not.

**One smaller thing found in the same place and fixed nowhere.** The entry at
the centre of all this quotes six and five literal characters of two live
GitHub App installation tokens, as evidence that two environment variables held
different values. Those tokens expired with the run that held them, so nothing
needs rotating and the fragments are far too short to be material. It is
recorded because the practice is the thing to correct rather than the string:
"two different values, confirmed by direct comparison" carries the entire
finding, and a public register is not the place to paste any part of a
credential. Not edited here for the collision reason above. The owner or the
engineer can drop the two fragments whenever #301 lands.

## INC-2026-10-15-stale-server-survives-restart-fourth-occurrence — the committed check was in the directory the whole time, and the run listed that directory with a glob that hid it (2026-10-15, frontend run)

**Observed by:** the frontend seat, 2026-10-15, during the Left-Behind Index
run, while running the charter's "check the register before you ship" step.

**The repeat, and it is the fourth.** `INC-2026-09-23-phantom-production-bug`,
`INC-2026-09-24-stale-server-kill-noop` and
`INC-2026-10-07-stale-server-third-occurrence` are the first three. The shape
is identical every time: a new `next start` loses the port to the server
already on it, dies into a log file with `EADDRINUSE`, and the subshell that
launched it returns success, so the shell reports nothing and the old process
keeps answering.

**The third entry's fix was real, and it was sitting right there.** That entry
ends on the rule that the fix for a missing check is committed code, and it
committed the code: `docs/design/harness/serve.sh`, whose second property is
reading the log for `EADDRINUSE` rather than trusting a backgrounded exit
