## INC-2026-10-18-twelve-seats-now-share-one-tmp-and-one-overwrote-another-seats-artifact — a scratch file written, clobbered by a concurrent seat, and published before the clobber was noticed (2026-10-18, exo seat)

**An eighth item for the inventory in
`INC-2026-10-18-the-hardening-stayed-in-the-runtime-the-seats-left`, and it
happened to this run rather than being found by it.**

**What happened.** This run composed its pull request description into
`/tmp/body.md`, ran a second command minutes later to amend it, and the
`assert` in that command failed because the file no longer held what this run
had written. It held another seat's prose, opening "This seat was woken by a
note from this product's project manager." The amend command had already
piped the file to `gh pr edit`, so **pull request #381 carried another seat's
text for about a minute** before the next turn restored it from a private
path.

**Why it is structural rather than careless.** In GitHub Actions each run had
its own ephemeral runner and therefore its own `/tmp`. On the company host,
twelve alexandria seats plus the seats of three other products run as the
same user on one machine, so `/tmp/<anything>` is a shared namespace with no
per-run prefix. There were twenty-four PM runs and nine writer runs on 2026-10-18
alone. A fixed filename in `/tmp` is now a race, and the race is silent: the
write succeeds, the read succeeds, and the content belongs to somebody else.

**Why it was caught.** Only because the amend command happened to assert on
its own content before replacing it. A run that wrote once and shipped once
would have published the other seat's text and never known. That is the
dangerous version and it is the common one, because most runs write a body
file once.

**The fix for every seat, and it is one rule.** A scratch file goes under a
path unique to this run, or it goes in the repository clone, which the runner
already makes fresh per run. Never a fixed name in `/tmp`.

```bash
# wrong on a shared host
cat > /tmp/body.md
# right, either of these
scratch=$(mktemp -d); cat > "$scratch/body.md"
cat > ./.git/exo-body.md     # inside the per-run clone, and never committed
```

**Filed as an ask rather than fixed in the runtime**, because a per-run
`TMPDIR` is the clean answer and it belongs in epitome's runner beside the
clone step. That is ask 7 of the 2026-10-18 entry in
`docs/agents/hq-relay.md`. The charter rule above is the part this seat can
ship, and it is in all twelve charters as of this pull request.

**One honest note on severity.** Nothing was lost and nothing reached a
reader, because the only artifact affected was a pull request description
that was corrected in the next turn and is reported in that description. The
reason it is registered anyway is the standing rule's reason: the mechanism
is live, it is silent, and twelve seats are exposed to it today.

## INC-2026-10-18-the-duplicate-candidate-register-is-not-in-the-charters-read-list — the register built to stop redrafting was four runs old and the ninth run redrafted anyway (2026-10-18, writer seat, ninth run)

**Observed** in this seat's own output. This run drafted
`docs/voice/2026-10-18-law-15-repairs.md`, four candidates for four
reader-facing lines that break canon law 15. Every one of the four surfaces
already had an open candidate: the home metric line in
`home-metric-line-2026-09-26.md`, twenty-two days old, the terms page in
`claim-repairs-2026-10-18.md`, and both llms.txt lines in
`llms-txt-2026-10-18.md`. All three earlier candidates are better. The home
one prints both numbers, what arrived and what was read in full, which is the
form law 15 explicitly asks a scale sentence to take, and this run's version
dropped the second number.

**Repeat.** Second occurrence of
`INC-2026-10-18-three-candidates-for-two-surfaces-in-one-day`, filed four runs
earlier the same day. The draft is withdrawn in the pull request that found
it.

**Why it repeated, and the answer is one line of a charter.** The fix for the
first occurrence was correct and it shipped:
`docs/voice/awaiting-her-word.md`, one row per open candidate, which says in
its own second paragraph that it is the first file a writer run opens, ahead
of the taste register. That sentence is in the file the run was supposed to
open. The run's charter names seven things to read before a candidate leaves
it, and that file is not among them, so a seat following its charter exactly
reads seven registers and not the eighth. The fix's own pull request said so
in its own words: "The charter's own list of what to read is a charter edit
and not this seat's to make, so the file names the duty in its own first
paragraph and the pull request asks for the charter line."

That is the fourth time this org has written a register whose only reader is
the register. Incident 20 is the shape, the claims register is the shape
pointed at surfaces, this is the shape pointed at a handoff, and the common
property is that the duty was written in the artifact that the duty was meant
to protect.

**Fix, in this pull request.** `docs/voice/check_voice.py candidates` reads
the register's open table against the candidate files the run's own diff adds,
and fails where a new candidate is for a surface already awaiting her word
without naming the candidate open on it. Naming it is the escape and it is the
register's own rule rather than a new one, because that is the difference
between superseding a draft and not knowing it exists. Proven both ways on the
withdrawn draft: it fired on all three surfaces, and passed once the draft
named the three files.

**Still open and not this seat's to close.** The charter line. A command the
run types is better than a sentence the run reads, and it is still enforced at
the reliability of a seat typing it until the wiring lands, which is the
ledger entry filed again in this pull request. The charter edit belongs to the
ExO seat and is asked for here rather than made.

**The honest part.** This run read the incident register, which is the
register that names `awaiting-her-word.md`, and read it after drafting rather
than before. The charter puts the register checks at the shipping step, which
is after the work by construction. That ordering is correct for a check and
wrong for a precondition, and it is why the fix here is a command on the diff
rather than another sentence telling a seat to read something first.
## INC-2026-10-18-press-recovery-content-anchor — the label and the date range were fixed to agree with each other, and nobody checked whether either agreed with the query that fills the body (2026-10-18, pm seat, found by alexandra-systems/mba)

**What happened.** This seat posted an urgent ask to the owner recommending
she run the press's recovery path to fill an unwritten weekly issue, priced
at "about the cost of one API call" against a permanent gap in a pricing
claim. `alexandra-systems/mba` checked that recommendation against
`pipeline/weekly.py` on `main` and found it wrong before the owner acted on
it: the recovery path does not recover the missing week.

**Why, mechanically.** `week_just_ended()` derives the issue's label and its
reader-facing date range from one shared anchor, the most recent Sunday
strictly before today. Every query that fills the issue's body
(`pipeline/weekly.py` lines 308, 315, 322, 325 and 327 as of this date) is
anchored to `now() - interval '7 days'` instead, independently of that
function. On the scheduled Monday run the two anchors agree closely enough
that nobody notices. Run on any other day, as a recovery always is, they
diverge: the label and date range describe the week that ended last Sunday,
while the content is whatever was created in the seven days up to the moment
the command runs. `weekly()` takes no week argument and the module's only
other entrypoint, `resend()`, only re-sends a row that already exists in
`digests`. There is no path in this module that writes a given week's actual
content on a day other than that week's own Monday. `digests` upserts on
week, so running the recovery writes the wrong content under the right
label, permanently, with no second chance.

**Why this is a repeat and not a new class.**
`INC-2026-09-28-press-week-label-off-schedule` is this same function, found
the same way, three weeks earlier: a date computation that is correct only
on the day the scheduled run fires and wrong on every day a recovery would
actually run on. That incident's fix unified the label and the date range
onto one anchor so they could never disagree with each other again. It did
not touch the queries that fill the body, because nothing at the time was
checking whether the body agreed with either of them. The general form named
in that entry, "a date function whose correctness depends on the day it runs
is a function that is correct in production and wrong in every recovery,"
applied to a part of the same function that the fix never reached.

**Why nothing caught it this time either.** The same reason as before: a
recovery runs only after something has already failed, which is the one
moment under the least testing attention, and the person weighing whether to
run it was reading the module's own docstring warning about the label and
treating that as the whole warning.

**Not fixed in this pull request, because it is not this seat's surface to
fix.** The engineer seat owns `pipeline/weekly.py`. What this entry fixes is
the record: the recommendation built on the missing check was withdrawn from
the ask it was made in before the owner acted on it, and the gap between the
module's two anchors is now named here rather than living only in a board
reply and a docstring that only covers half of it.

**Repaired 2026-10-26 by the engineer seat, which is the surface this entry
was addressed to.** `gather` takes a window, `week_window(week)` builds the
exact span the Monday cron would have read, and both callers that write an
issue pass it, so the queries this entry cites by line number are now anchored
to the same week as the label above them. `weekly` also takes the week by name
(`modal run pipeline/weekly.py::weekly --week 2026-W41`), which is the verb the
withdrawn recovery needed and did not have, and a named-week run mails nobody:
it writes the row and prints the `resend` command. The property is pinned in
`tests/test_press_backfill.py::test_the_scheduled_path_reads_the_week_it_prints`,
which fails on any return to the old anchor. Two things this does not close.
Nothing has rehearsed it, because the Modal workspace has been disabled since
2026-10-23, and the module's own deploy command runs `rehearse` before
`modal deploy`, so the rehearsal is the gate and it is in the deploy path
rather than skipped. And whether 2026-W41 should be written at all is still
the owner's call, unchanged by this: what changed is that the command now
writes the week it names.

**The lesson for this seat.** A recommendation that prices an action in cost
and names what it buys back is a claim that the action does what it says.
This seat priced a command without reading whether it wrote the content its
label claims to describe. The next ask that recommends running a one-line
recovery reads the function behind it first, not just the function's own
docstring warning, which can describe its own history correctly and still
not cover everything true about the function around it.

## INC-2026-10-18-a-pass-is-not-a-pull-request — one PM seat opened fifteen pull requests in one day, thirteen of them changing nothing but one tracker file (2026-10-18, pm seat, six-hour pass)

**Observed** at the start of this pass: `gh pr list` showed fifteen open pull
requests authored by this seat alone from today, `#332`, `#335`, `#362`,
`#365`, `#367`, `#369`, `#371`, `#373` through `#380`. Eleven of them touch
only `docs/sprints/pending.md`, each the record of a single event-bus wake
answered on the board rather than in the tree. None merged; three were
restating the same confirmed finding a second and third time (`#374`, `#378`,
`#380`).

**The rule that produced it.** `docs/standards/pm.md` §1 still says one run
makes one pull request. §17 turned a run into a pass that fires on every
board write. The two rules were written for different cadences and nobody
reconciled them when the second one shipped, so a pass that answers one
narrow event correctly, by this charter's own instructions, still opens a
whole pull request to say so.

**Not a first telling.** `alexandra-systems/mba`'s note to HQ's own PM,
read in this seat's inbox this morning, named the same shape across the
whole portfolio: twenty-six of fifty-nine open pull requests change nothing
but a tracker file. This seat's own prior pass (`#380`) already named its own
fourteen-PR count on the board without filing it here. Recording it now
rather than a second time unrecorded.

**Why it costs more than the clutter.** Every one of these PRs is this
seat's own, so Tier B condition 1 bars this seat from merging any of them no
matter which tier the diff actually sits in. A prior pass (`#374`) verified
six of them as genuinely Tier A by `git merge-tree`, clean against `main`,
and still nobody but the owner or a chair can clear them. The queue this
seat exists to move instead grows by one every time the bus wakes it, and
the growth is indistinguishable from real backlog to anyone reading PR count
alone.

**Fix, not taken here.** Reconciling §1 and §17 is a standards change,
HQ's to make or the owner's to direct, not this seat's to invent. What this
pass did instead: closed two of its own fifteen as superseded by a third,
named the six Tier-A-clean ones as a batchable merge for the owner or a
chair, and is filing this entry so the next pass reads the pattern here
rather than rediscovering it as a fresh surprise.

## INC-2026-10-18-tier-c-carve-out-misread-a-sixth-time — PR #367 held a green budget-gate fix for a prompt file that is not a seat's authority (2026-10-18, pm seat)

**What happened.** `docs/standards/pm.md` §21 (owner, 2026-10-05) and §10's own
amendment note say a PM merges every tier in its own company except a change
to a seat's own authority, spend, an account, or a secret. `INC-2026-10-09-tier-c-carve-out-misread-for-four-days`
already recorded five passes over four days reading `prompts/` as a single
Tier C path regardless of that carve-out, on `prompts/distill.md` and
`prompts/distill-practices.md`. This seat's own pass at ~06:46 UTC today
(PR #367, reviewing PR #363) made the identical read on a third file:
"Tier C names `prompts/` as a charter path on its own, independent of the
check result, so even a green run on this diff would not be mine to merge."
`prompts/digest.md` carries no seat's authority, no tier definition, no spend,
account or secret; it is the writer seat's generator prompt, the exact kind of
content prompt the 2026-10-09 entry already named as outside Tier C.

**Why it is a repeat and not a new mistake.** Same shorthand, same wrong
conclusion, same unchecked assumption ("prompts/ is Tier C") that the standing
incident already diagnosed and named a fix for: read the carve-out sentence
against the specific file in the diff, not the remembered shape of the
directory. The fix did not stick across the four-day gap between the two
incidents, and nothing short of a check run against the actual sentence
would have caught it before a PM pass repeated it.

**What this run found and did differently.** PR #363 closed on its own
(superseded by PR #366, "build on #363," confirmed with
`git log --oneline origin/alexandria-writer/2026-10-18-message-payload-audit ^HEAD`
printing nothing), and PR #366 fixed exactly the red check #367 held on: the
single `checks.yml` job (`digest request fits the model's budget`) is green,
`mergeStateStatus: CLEAN`, not a draft, no `hold` label, no comment, no review,
and `gh pr diff --name-only 366` shows `docs/agents/incidents.md`,
`docs/ideas.md`, `docs/voice/ban-list.md`, `docs/voice/canon.md`, two new
`docs/voice/reviews/` files, and `prompts/digest.md` — no seat-authority path,
no spend, no secret. Merged under Tier B (`gh pr merge 366 --merge`,
`99a1405`).

**Not fixed here, named instead.** A command that answers the carve-out
question from the actual file in the diff, the way `tools/check-tier.sh`
already does per the 2026-10-09 entry's own account of PR #253, would stop
this from costing a sixth pass. This repo has no such script yet
(`ls tools/` shows no `check-tier.sh` or equivalent); filed in `docs/ideas.md`
is the engineer's to size, not this seat's to build.

## INC-2026-10-23-a-voice-gates-first-firing-is-green-for-a-false-reason — two consecutive runs built a check that passed on an artifact violating the rule it checks, and both passes were caught by one more reading rather than by anything in the loop (2026-10-23, writer seat, run 42)

**The repeat.** On 2026-10-18 the writer seat shipped
`docs/voice/check_voice.py taste` and it passed on its first firing, 31 of 31
rulings green. The run nearly shipped it. Her 2026-09-29 ruling was green
because two of its six verdicts are anchored to headings she approved herself
and both quotes resolved, while the sixth verdict of that same ruling was
being broken on three live reader-facing surfaces at that moment. That is
recorded inside the review of that day as "the first green run was false, and
that is the finding worth keeping" and it was never filed here.

On 2026-10-23 the same seat shipped `check_voice.py firstuse` and its first
cut cleared three real violations in one sentence of
`site/content/issues/2026-W39.md`:

> The newer work shows that an on-policy expert-correction pipeline, which
> rewrites only the failing turn in the weaker model's rollout, preserves its
> planning style and restores performance where imitation alone fails.

Three club words, one relative clause, and the clause defines the pipeline.
The check asked whether a gloss marker appeared anywhere in the term's first
sentence, so all three passed. The issue defines none of the three anywhere.

**Why it is one incident and not two coincidences.** Both checks failed the
same way, and the way is structural rather than careless. Each one asked
whether the right KIND of evidence was present in the right NEIGHBOURHOOD,
and each one then passed on an artifact that had such evidence nearby meaning
something else. The taste gate found a quote in the generator and concluded a
ruling was held. The first-use gate found a clause in the sentence and
concluded a term was glossed. Neither had bound its evidence to the subject it
was making a claim about.

**What caught it, both times.** A seat reading the output and disbelieving it.
Nothing in the loop. Both runs had a passing gate, a clean selfcheck and a
green suite, and in both cases the only thing between a false green and a
shipped false green was one more reading by the run that wrote it. That is the
part worth fixing and this entry does not fix it.

**The repair that did land, both times.** Bind the evidence to the subject.
The taste gate's rows can now inherit a command's verdict on the artifact
instead of resting on a quote of the rule. The first-use gate now reads the
window from the term onward and asks only about the next few characters,
because a definition arrives adjacent to the word it defines. Both repairs
turned a green gate red for a true reason.

**The standards already say this, and that is the finding rather than a
proposal.** The reflex here is to ask HQ for a new rule, and checking first
shows two that already cover it, both in the `any` section every seat is told
to read before working.

`L-A39` is the class: "A freshness check that tests for presence answers a
different question." Both gates tested for presence. The taste gate asked
whether a quote of a ruling was present in the generator and answered a
question about the generator instead of about the issue. The first-use gate
asked whether a gloss marker was present in a sentence and answered a question
about the sentence instead of about the term.

`L-A21` is the procedure: "every gate is tested against an artifact known to
fail it before the gate is trusted." That clause, followed, catches both. It
was followed on `firstuse`, which is why three fixtures exist and why green
was proved before red. It was not followed on `taste` five days earlier, where
the first firing was green and believed until a second reading.

So this seat does not need a new standard. It had two and read neither before
working, which is what `L-A4` calls a register defect and what `L-A9` has
already been written about twice. The concrete duty that would have changed
both runs is one line in this seat's charter, which is not this seat's surface
and is filed in `docs/ideas.md` for the ExO seat: a writer run that adds or
changes a command in `docs/voice/check_voice.py` names, in its review, the
artifact it constructed that the new check SHOULD fail, and the exit code it
got. Green with no such artifact named is not a result.

**Not a repeat, recorded because the standing rule admits no judgment call.**
`python3 tools/board.py show --seat writer` answered
`503 the board's database is unreachable` on this run's first call and
succeeded on the retry a few minutes later. The run read its lane off
`docs/voice/awaiting-her-word.md` in the interval and lost nothing. The
existing entries on board 503s, `INC-2026-09-28-board-run-reports-still-503`
and `INC-2026-09-29-board-run-reports-503-third-run`, are both about
`POST /api/runs` refusing writes across many hours. This was a GET, it
recovered on its own, and it is filed here only so the count is complete.

## INC-2026-10-23-a-404-was-reported-as-a-mystery-while-the-body-named-a-total-outage — the third time this org read an HTTP status as the fact and left the explanation unread (2026-10-23, engineer seat)

Recorded under the standing rule. The two prior entries are
`INC-2026-09-20-the-arxiv-406-is-rate-limiting-wearing-the-wrong-status-code`
and `INC-2026-10-17-a-403-was-recorded-as-a-measured-death-and-the-gate-never-
asked-the-production-client`, and the second of those closes by naming the next
place it would happen. It happened somewhere neither of them looked: not in a
tool that reads someone else's feed, but in the guardrail that reads this
company's own platform.

**What happened.** At 23:08 UTC today `python3 tools/delivery_health.py`
reported eight surfaces. One of them read `FAILING mcp /mcp returned an
unexpected HTTP 404`. Two of them read `ok`: `pipeline  ingesting and
distilling within 2 days`, and `deploy  a deploy is pending and still inside
the 24h window`.

One `curl` of the same URL returned, as its entire body,
`modal-http: workspace <id> is disabled`.

Every cron in `pipeline/` and the MCP server are apps in that one workspace.
The whole compute layer of this company was switched off, and the report said
one route was missing and the pipeline was fine.

**How long, and how it was timed.** The deploy surface's own evidence dates it
without needing a log. `ingest` last ran at 2026-10-23 11:02 UTC and `triage`
at 12:00 UTC, both today and both normal. `interpret` is scheduled at 14:00
and last ran 2026-10-22. `distill` is scheduled at 15:00 and last ran
2026-10-22. So the workspace was serving at 12:00 UTC and gone by 14:00, and
the outage was about nine hours old when this run met it. Two scheduled jobs
had already been missed. `distill_pending` stood at 3,680.

**Why the status code was not enough, stated precisely.** Modal's HTTP edge
answers for every app in a workspace, including the ones it will not route.
It returns 404 with a one-line plain-text body prefixed `modal-http:`, and
that line is the only place the cause is written down. `check_mcp` fetched the
body, bound it to a local named `body`, used it on the connection-error path,
and dropped it on every other path in favour of the integer. So the probe held
the answer and reported the symptom. This is the same defect as the two prior
entries with the polarity reversed: those read a status code as a fact about
something it was not about, and this one declined to read anything else while
the fact sat in hand.

**Why `pipeline` read green, which is the worse half.** `judge_pipeline`'s unit
is staleness and its window is two days. That is the right unit for the
failure it was built for, which is a cron that runs and produces nothing. It
is structurally blind to a platform that stops, because for two days after the
last cron that will ever run, every row it judges is still fresh. The same
blindness is in `deploy`, which reads what the last run recorded: an outage
freezes that number rather than changing it, so the surface keeps reporting
the last healthy answer indefinitely. Neither surface was wrong about what it
measures. Nothing measured whether the platform was up.

This is incident 24's shape again, and the org has now met it on the press
(incident 24), on the till
(`INC-2026-10-18-the-till-had-no-outside-observer`), and today on the compute
every other surface depends on. Each time, the question was answered from
inside the system's own records, and each time an outsider's single request
would have answered it in one line.

**What it cost.** Nothing recoverable was lost: the corpus is intact, the
press had already printed 2026-W42 on Monday, and the two missed jobs are
daily ones that catch up. What it cost is the nine hours, and what it would
have cost is unbounded, because nothing in this org was going to notice. The
daily standup reads this command, and this command was going to keep saying
the pipeline was ingesting and distilling for another day and a half. The
first surface that would have turned red on its own is `press`, next Monday.

**What this seat did about it.** `tools/delivery_health.py` gains a `compute`
surface that asks Modal's edge directly, a `modal_edge_outage` classifier that
reads the body the probe already had, and an outage fact threaded into
`judge_pipeline` so that fresh rows cannot read green while the platform is
confirmed down. The MCP probe now quotes Modal instead of paraphrasing the
status code. Five tests in `tests/test_delivery_health.py` hold it, including
the direction it must not go: a request that never arrived is `unknown` and
never `failing`, because an alarm that cries wolf about its own sandbox's
network is one nobody reads on the day it is right.

**What this seat could not do.** Re-enabling the workspace is an account action
on Modal and no agent seat holds that. It is in the ledger as `urgent`, and it
is the only thing on today's list that needs the owner's hands.

**The generalisation, for the ExO.** Every one of this org's delivery surfaces
reads an artifact the system itself wrote. That was the whole point of
guardrail 4, and it was a real advance over reading `gh run list`. But a record
written by a dead system is indistinguishable from a record written by a
healthy idle one, and the only cure is a probe that talks to the platform
rather than to its output. Guardrail 4 says read the artifact, not the
scheduler. Today adds: and ask the platform whether it is there, because an
artifact cannot tell you it has stopped being written.

## INC-2026-10-23-the-generator-is-not-on-the-list-of-files-checked-for-edit-damage — a file carried four blocks of its own text twice, and the checker built for exactly that damage does not read it and would not have caught this form of it (2026-10-23, writer seat, run 43)

**What happened.** `prompts/digest.md` on main was carrying four blocks of its
own text twice: two rule bullets, one slot instruction and one single line,
each written in beside the copy the file already held. Three of the four first
copies end in the middle of a sentence, which is what identifies the cause as
an edit that inserted replacement text and did not remove what it replaced.

One of the four was not cosmetic. The duplicated slot instruction opened a
second curly brace, so the file's brace depth never returned to zero after
line 1145. Every slot from the reading list to the sign-off was nested inside
an instruction block that never closed, including the closing line canon law 10
requires to print verbatim and last, in a file whose own line 502 tells the
model that text in curly braces is an instruction to it and is replaced by its
own words.

**Why it is a repeat and not a finding.** This is the same class as the
2026-09-24 damage in this register, recorded in this file's own header note:
"this file carried two verbatim copies of incidents 19 and 20, from a merge
that appended entries the file already held." `tools/check_registers.py` was
built in answer to it. Two things about that answer are the actual incident.

1. **The criterion is met and the file is not on the list.** That checker's own
   comment says the criterion for inclusion is not that a file is famous, it is
   "that more than one seat appends to it, because that is what produces the
   anchor contention". The list has grown to sixteen files. `prompts/digest.md`
   is the most-appended file in the writer seat's custody, 101 commits in forty
   days by the canon's own count, and it is not on it.
2. **The damage test is narrower than the damage it was built for.** The test
   is `CONFLICT`, seven characters of git marker at the start of a line. The
   2026-09-24 damage was not a conflict marker. It was clean duplicated text.
   So the gate built in response to that incident catches the loud form of the
   failure and never the form that caused it, and has been green over this
   class of damage in sixteen files for twenty-nine days.

**Why nothing else saw it.** Three gates read this file every time this seat
runs and all three read past it. The weighing gate measures its token cost and
passed it. The taste gate finds every one of her rulings present in it and
scored 27 of 31 green. The enforcements command verifies forty-six quoted
anchors inside it and reported zero missing. Every one of them was reading a
file that disagreed with itself about where its own instructions ended, because
each asks a question about the file's contents and none asks whether the file
is well formed.

**Blameless postmortem.** No seat did anything the loop told it not to. The
trimming edit that produced the pair at line 1946 was following the weighing
gate's own rule that dates are this seat's notes rather than the model's
instructions, and it wrote the trimmed sentence in correctly. What was missing
is the step after an edit: every charter warns the seat that is about to
append, and the thing that reads the result afterwards exists for sixteen files
and not for this one. The 2026-09-24 entry made this exact observation in its
own words, "what is missing is not the fix but the looking", and then added a
checker whose list this file never joined.

**Fixed in this pull request.** The four blocks are removed, no operative
clause among them, brace depth back to zero, 34,364 tokens to 34,043, and the
per-issue worst case from $0.1479 to $0.1476 against a $0.15 ceiling the build
fails over. `docs/voice/check_voice.py generator` is the instrument, with three
detectors and six named fixtures: green on the repaired file and a clean
fixture, red on the file as main carried it naming all four blocks with their
line numbers, and red on three fixtures holding one defect each.

**Open, and it is the engineer's edit rather than this seat's.** Adding
`prompts/digest.md` to `REGISTERS` in `tools/check_registers.py`, and widening
that checker's damage test past the git marker to the duplicated block so the
other sixteen files get the same cover, is filed in the ledger with the
measured finding. The writer seat does not write pipeline or tools code.

## INC-2026-10-23-the-law-quoted-its-own-evidence-and-the-gate-could-not-read-it — canon law 15's cited string is the first line of the public archive, twenty-eight days after the masthead was repaired (2026-10-23, writer seat, run 44)

**What happened.** Canon law 15, her ruling of 2026-09-25, cites exactly one
string as its evidence and names it as a masthead: "read in full and distilled
weekly" on every issue ever sent, against 166 full reads out of 8,956 papers
held. `MASTHEAD` in `pipeline/weekly.py` was repaired. On 2026-10-23 the third
line of `site/content/issues/2026-W39.md` still said it, and
`site/lib/issues-core.js` makes that file the live public text of the one week
the archive publishes: "the record decides which weeks exist, the committed
file decides the text of any week that has one."

So the sentence the law quotes as the thing that must never happen is the first
line a reader of the public archive meets, and has been for twenty-eight days.

**Why it is a repeat, and of what.** `docs/standards/lessons.md` L-A21 is the
company law for this exact failure and it is a vendored copy, so it was written
from a defect that had already happened elsewhere. Its words: "its scope is
narrower than its subject: a law can fire on schedule, pass its own audit, and
miss, because it is pointed at the wrong place." It then gives the test. "Name
one change that would break what this gate governs, then ask whether the gate
would have seen that change, not whether it would have fired on it."

`docs/voice/check_voice.py reading` was built for law 15. Its surface list held
`pipeline/weekly.py`, the module that writes the NEXT issue, and held no issue
that module had already produced. A masthead repaired in the module is repaired
for every week the press has not written yet and for no week it already did.
The gate was red on four `site/app` lines the whole time, so it never looked
like a gate that was passing, which is how it kept attention off its scope.

Three further links, each a seat already knowing the half it was holding.

- The hole was written into the check's own docstring on the day it was built:
  "a sentence that says read in full over a number that came from the ingest
  field passes here and is a worse version of the same lie." It was not a
  hypothetical. It was already in print when the sentence predicting it was
  typed. **A known gap recorded beside the gate that has it is a gap nothing
  closes, because the record reads as handled.** That is L-A9 with the register
  and the gate in one file.
- `INC-2026-10-18-a-drafted-copy-repair-sat-unset-for-twenty-two-days` is the
  same law, the same word and the same month on a different surface. That one
  was drafted and unset. This one was never drafted, because nothing saw it.
- L-A24's stated consequence is the mechanism here in one line: "only an
  outside observer reading the artifact catches the missing run, because a
  scheduler reports its own intentions." Swap run for string. The module
  reports its own intention and the archive holds the outcome.

**The second blindness, which compounded with the first.** `READING` exempts
"read in full", and it must: that is the one act the word may name, and "164
papers read in full" is both true and the sentence the law asks for. Between a
surface list that excluded the archive and a regex that excluded the phrase,
the check built for law 15 could not see the words law 15 quotes.

**Fixed in this pull request, in `docs/voice/check_voice.py`.** `reading` takes
`ARCHIVE_GLOBS` on top of the surface list, so it reads 63 surfaces where it
read 61, and the first firing reported the line. The exemption now holds for
the count form and not the cadence form: attached to a count, read in full is a
fact, and attached to a cadence it is a claim about everything that arrived
that week. The globs go to `reading` alone, because `claims` reads the same
list and an issue body's sentences are claims about the research rather than
about our artifact.

**Not fixed here, and named rather than left.** The line itself is drafted at
`docs/voice/archive-masthead-2026-10-23.md` and is the frontend seat's to set,
because `site/` is not the writer seat's surface. Until it is set the archive
carries the sentence and the gate is red about it, which is the correct state
of both.

**The generalisable half, which is a scope question rather than a string
question.** Every gate this seat owns reads `site/app`, `site/lib`,
`site/emails` and two pipeline modules. The archive was on none of their lists,
and the archive is the only surface in the product where a repair cannot reach
backwards. L-A21's test applied to the rest of them is work this run did for
`reading` and did not do for `claims`, deliberately and with the reason filed,
and `docs/ideas.md` carries the question for the ExO seat whose register it is.

**Blameless note.** No seat skipped a step. The masthead repair was correct and
complete for the file it was in. The gate was built after the repair and
pointed at the file the repair had touched, which is the natural place to point
it and is the trap: a gate written in the same breath as a fix inherits the
fix's scope, and the fix's scope was the module. Ban list 131 and 132.

## INC-2026-10-23-the-exo-seats-own-draft-aged-four-hours-and-a-handoff-was-its-only-reader — the seat that keeps this register produced the fourth sighting of the class it already holds (2026-10-23, exo seat, about its own earlier run the same day)

**Observed by:** the PM seat, in the handoff that triggered this run. Its
words, attached to the wake rather than filed anywhere: "one of your pull
requests is an open draft with no live run behind it, so no gate can reach it.
GitHub refuses to merge a draft at all."

**What happened.** PR #404
(`alexandria-exo/2026-10-23-message`) opened at 2026-10-23 19:06 UTC carrying
43 commits and 22 files, which is the work of three unmerged ExO runs. Its
description still read "Observation in progress. This description will be
rewritten before `gh pr ready`." The run never came back to rewrite it and
never called `gh pr ready`. Four hours later it was still a draft, which means
every line of three runs' work was unreachable by any gate, by the owner's
merge, and by the next run of the seat that wrote it.

**This is the fourth sighting of a class this file already names.**
`INC-2026-10-18-the-ship-first-rules-closing-half-went-unrun-and-an-empty-draft-aged-two-days`
recorded the third, against the engineer seat, and its own heading says it was
the third. The company standard has had a rule id for it since then, L-A32, "a
run is over when its artifact is reachable, not when it is written." So the
law existed, the incident existed, the lesson had an id, and the seat that
reads all three of those files every run produced the defect anyway, in the
same week.

**Why, stated as a property rather than as a lapse, because the interesting
half is that every gate was present.** The ship-first rule has two halves and
they are asymmetric in a way nothing in the org had noticed. The opening half
runs at the start of a run, when the run has budget and a plan, and it is also
the half every charter writes about at length. The closing half runs at the
end, which is exactly when a run is out of turns, out of context, or simply
finished with the part that felt like the work. A rule whose compliance step
is scheduled for the moment of greatest exhaustion is a rule with a structural
failure rate, and the four sightings are spread across three different seats,
which is what tells you it is the rule's shape and not a seat's discipline.

The second property: **the failure is silent to its own author and invisible
to everyone else.** A draft PR looks exactly like live work. Nobody can
distinguish "this run is still going" from "this run died at turn 90" by
looking, which is the sentence the 2026-10-18 entry already wrote about the
engineer's PR and which is why that one aged 48 hours. This one aged four,
and the only reason it aged four rather than four days is that a PM run
happened to be awake, happened to look at the open-PR list, and attached the
finding to this seat's next wake.

**What this run did.** Carried #404 forward into #411 with the containment
proof the charter requires, closed #404 as superseded, and shipped ready. The
work is not lost and the chain is now five deep, which is reported in #411's
description as the charter's depth rule requires.

**CORRECTION, 2026-10-24, by the next run of the same seat: the cause written
above is wrong, and the evidence was one API call away while it was being
written.** The board's run record for that session reads `exit: 1`, 48 turns,
started 19:04:14Z and ended 19:09:05Z. **The run did not decline to come
back. It crashed, four minutes and fifty-eight seconds after opening the
draft, at 24% of its 200-turn cap.**

So two sentences above are false and they are the load-bearing ones. "The run
never came back to rewrite it" describes a choice; there was none. And the
diagnosis built on it — "a rule whose compliance step is scheduled for the
moment of greatest exhaustion" — cannot apply to a run that was nowhere near
exhausted. The ship-first analysis may still be right about the other three
sightings. It is not what happened here, and this entry was the fourth of
four, so the pattern it completed is now three sightings and one crash.

**The part that is worth more than the correction.** This entry contains the
sentence "nobody can distinguish 'this run is still going' from 'this run
died at turn 90' by looking." That was true of looking at a pull request and
false of the organization, because a field named `exit` had been sitting on
the board since 2026-10-18. The entry recorded that a distinction was
unavailable and then asserted one of its two sides anyway. **Where a register
says a distinction cannot be made, no later sentence in the same entry may
depend on either side of it**; the entry stops at the ambiguity and names what
would settle it.

Why the evidence was not reached: the charter that run obeys defines failure
observation as `gh run list`, which has not been able to see a seat since
2026-10-17. The full account is
`INC-2026-10-24-the-receipt-we-asked-for-was-built-and-no-charter-was-pointed-at-it`.
The two sightings this correction depends on are registered there as well,
because neither was recorded at the time.

**What the org should grow from it, and this seat is deliberately not writing
the fix into its own charter alone.** Four sightings across three seats is a
machinery problem, not a prose problem, and the honest observation is that the
one thing that has ever caught this class is another seat reading the open-PR
list. That worked twice now, both times by the PM. The PM's charter already
reads the run list daily. Making the draft-age check an explicit line in that
pass, with a threshold and a message, turns the two lucky catches into a
mechanism. That is the PM seat's charter and not this seat's surface, so it is
filed as a finding here and named in #411's description rather than edited in.
What this seat did edit is its own charter, which now says the closing half of
ship-first is the step a run budgets turns for rather than the step it has
left over.

## INC-2026-10-23-a-registers-summary-contradicted-its-own-table-four-times-in-twelve-days — the prose under a data table is a measurement with no date on it (2026-10-23, exo seat, about docs/agents/quality-claims.md)

**Observed** while adding the home page metric row that the PM seat handed
over. `docs/agents/quality-claims.md` closes with a section called "What this
table says as a whole", and its most emphatic sentence, in bold, read: "Every
claim that holds is about the corpus, and every claim that fails is about the
skills."

That sentence was written on 2026-10-18. On 2026-10-11, seven days earlier,
the same register had moved "the library grows every day" out of `held` and
into `contradicted`. That claim is about the corpus. On 2026-10-18 itself, in
the same commit as the sentence, the register added "each week the library
becomes an issue" as `contradicted`. That claim is also about the corpus. So
the sentence was falsified by two rows of its own table, one of which was
added by the same edit.

**The repeat, and the count is four in twelve days.** All four are the same
page and the same shape.

1. 2026-10-11, the growth row sat at `held` on a count taken 2026-09-29 while
   the number that falsified it was on a public endpoint the whole time.
2. 2026-10-18, the field map named a claim shape the table had no row for,
   for seven days, across five public surfaces including the pricing page.
3. 2026-10-18, the count sentence said "three hold" for the seven days after
   the growth row stopped holding.
4. 2026-10-23, this one, in the sentence the page itself calls "the single
   most useful sentence on this page".

The register recorded the first three in its own prose, correctly diagnosed
them as one mechanism, and wrote the fix as a fourth step in the ExO charter's
§3g. None of the three was ever filed here, which is why nothing counted them
together, and the standing rule at the top of this file says a repeat is
recorded at the moment it repeats with no exceptions. Three went unrecorded.
That omission is itself the thing the standing rule calls an incident, and it
is recorded now.

**Why it keeps happening.** The diagnosis already in the register is right as
far as it goes: the page has a method half and a data half and a summary that
counts the data half, so a run editing one does not see the other two. The
fourth instance adds the part that diagnosis was missing. **Every number in
the table carries the moment it was taken. The prose underneath carries no
date at all.** A reader discounts a stale measurement automatically because
its date is next to it, and reads a stale conclusion as current forever,
because conclusions do not look like measurements. The decay is not slower in
the prose. It is only invisible.

**Fixed in this pull request.** Three edits, and the first is the general one.
Every claim the register makes about its own table now carries its date in the
same sentence, the way every row in the Measured column does. The counts say
"recounted from the table 2026-10-23". The distribution sentence is replaced
by a narrower one that is true, "every claim that holds is about the corpus,
and no claim about the skills holds", with its date in its first line and an
explicit note that the reverse does not follow. And the three earlier
instances are gathered into one section on the page so the next run sees a
count rather than three asides.

**What the org grows from it, for any register with a summary.** A file that
holds both measurements and conclusions about those measurements needs the
same discipline on both, and the discipline is cheap: date the conclusion in
its own sentence. This seat keeps eight such files. The rule goes in
`docs/agents/registers.md` rather than only here, because the defect is a
property of the file shape and not of this one page.

## INC-2026-10-23-the-routing-policy-said-free-for-a-pipeline-that-had-moved-to-a-paid-provider — the third register of this seat's own contradicted by a receipt of this seat's own (2026-10-23, exo seat)

**Observed** while running the new dated-conclusion rule across this seat's
registers, in the same run that wrote the rule.

**What happened.** `docs/agents/model-routing.md` is this seat's register and
names this seat as the owner of the routing policy. Its table was headed "The
routing table (current policy)", carried no date, and its first row read
"Pipeline judgment (triage, distill, interpret) | gpt-oss-120b (Groq, $0)".

ADR-32 moved the press to Moonshot. `pipeline/budget.py` has read
`PRIMARY_PROVIDER = "moonshot"` and `PRIMARY_MODEL = "kimi-k2.6"` since, and
the public delivery receipt reported `kimi-k2.6` for press, triage and
interpret at 2026-10-23T23:44:17Z. Moonshot is paid. So the page told every
reader that the most expensive half of the pipeline ran for nothing, on a page
whose purpose is to route work to open models where they suffice, and the three
Groq models it named are now fallbacks that `budget.py`'s own comment says
cannot print a weekly issue at all.

**The repeat, and the count is three.** On 2026-10-11 the growth row in
`quality-claims.md` sat at `held` on a count taken 2026-09-29 while the number
that falsified it was on the public receipt hourly. On 2026-10-18 the
weekly-issue claim had no row in the same register while the same receipt
published the field that measures it. This is the third, and all three have the
identical shape: **the register holding the claim and the receipt holding the
number are both this seat's, and nothing had ever read one against the other.**
The register itself wrote that sentence about itself on 2026-10-11 and the
lesson did not travel one file sideways.

**Why, and the honest part is that a law already covered it.** Since 2026-09-24
`docs/agents/runtime-changes.md` names a provider or model change as a runtime
change, and the ExO charter's §2 runs a `pipeline/` diff every week looking for
exactly those commits. That audit asks whether a merged PR explained the change,
whether there was a smoke run, and whether there was a rehearsal. It does not
ask whether the register that names the model was updated, so the audit could
pass in full on the week the page went false and did.

**Fixed in this pull request.** The row is corrected with the receipt and the
code as its evidence, the heading carries a date, and every row now carries the
date it was last verified. The reviewer-panel row carries no date on purpose,
because this run did not re-verify it against `pipeline/panel*.py`, and a row
with no date is a row the page is not currently claiming. The two verification
commands are written into the page.

**What is still open, and it is a charter edit the next run should weigh rather
than one this run should make blind.** The §2 machinery diff should ask a fifth
question of any commit touching a model or a provider: which register names
this model, and was it updated in the same commit. Three instances is enough to
know the shape and this run has already spent its three improvements, so it is
named here rather than written in, which is the charter's own rule about an
improvement needing an observed trigger and a ranked slot.

## INC-2026-10-24-the-receipt-we-asked-for-was-built-and-no-charter-was-pointed-at-it — two seat failures went unrecorded and a third was recorded with the wrong cause, while the field that explained all three sat unread for six days (2026-10-24, exo seat)

**Enforced at:** prompts/exo-agent.md §2a-0 and §2b, prompts/pm-agent.md §1f.

**What happened, in the order it happened.**

On 2026-10-11 this seat wrote an entry in `docs/agents/hq-relay.md` titled
"The event bus starts a third of our runs and reports no outcome, so no seat
can audit them." Its ask was one sentence with four acceptable answers: "have
the bus write each session's outcome somewhere the target repository can read:
a commit status, a check run, a repository_dispatch back with the result, or a
row in the board. Any of the four closes it."

**HQ built the fourth one.** `GET $BOARD_API_URL/api/board/<company>` now
returns a `runs` array, one row per host session, carrying `seat`, `trigger`,
`started_at`, `ended_at`, `turns`, `model`, `exit`, `refusal`, `pr_url`,
`run_url` and `report`. The oldest row on 2026-10-24 began 2026-10-18T12:40Z,
so the receipt has existed for six days.

**Nobody here changed a charter.** The relay entry is still marked
undelivered. `docs/agents/unowned-duties.md` still carries the duty as
unowned on the grounds that the evidence does not exist. ExO charter §2 still
opened with `gh run list --workflow=<name>`, §2b still filtered on
`workflowName|endswith("-agent")`, §2c still called a `workflow_dispatch`
count "the single cleanest measure", and PM charter §1f still began every
standup with `gh run list --limit 30` "across all agent workflows". Decision
056 had retired every one of those schedules on 2026-10-17.

**What it cost, three items, none of which was visible to any seat.**

1. `alexandria-exo`, 2026-10-23T19:04:14Z, `window:message`, 48 turns of a
   200 cap, **exit 1**. Unrecorded until today.
2. `alexandria-pm`, 2026-10-23T19:09:06Z, `window:message`, **1 turn, exit
   1**, seven seconds long, started one second after the exo run ended. The
   PM subscribes to `run.failed`, so this is almost certainly the triage run
   for item 1, and it died before it could read anything. Unrecorded until
   today. **The failure-reporting path failed on the failure it was woken
   for, and that is why item 3 happened.**
3. `INC-2026-10-23-the-exo-seats-own-draft-aged-four-hours-and-a-handoff-was-its-only-reader`
   was written four hours later, by this seat, about item 1, and attributed
   it to a run that chose not to return at the end of its budget. A
   correction is now in that entry.

**Why it is a repeat, and of what.** This is L-A16, **configured is not in
effect**, which this organization has now paid for in both directions. The
usual direction is a capability declared and never switched on. This is the
inverse and it is the more expensive one: **a capability switched on and
never declared.** Nothing looked broken, no gate went red, and the only
symptom was that every report of fleet health came back clean.

**The company already has the law for this, and it arrived in this
repository while this pull request was open.** `docs/standards/lessons.md`
was re-vendored from HQ as PR #417, merged 2026-10-24, and it carries
**L-A80 — a read that succeeds with nothing in it is not a reading**: "a
surface that answers successfully and empty cannot be told apart from a
healthy and empty world, and every reader will take the second reading,
because that is the one that asks nothing of them." Its two cited sources
are a dead Atom feed returning HTTP 200 with zero entries and HQ's own
`/api/scorecard` returning `weeks: []`. **This is the third source and the
first one that is not an instrument.**

That difference is the only thing worth adding to the law rather than
restating it. L-A80's remedy is "a zero states which of the two it is, and
an instrument that cannot tell them apart does not ship as an instrument,"
which is advice to whoever builds the instrument. `gh run list` is not ours
to change and it is not wrong: it correctly reports that no `*-agent`
workflow ran. **When the empty read comes from a tool you do not own, the
only available remedy is on the reading side** — the charter has to name the
source's liveness and re-point the command when the source retires, because
no amount of care at the call site can make somebody else's zero speak. That
extension is going up through `docs/agents/hq-relay.md`.

L-A83, *a rolling window with a hole in it is not a window*, lands on the
same evidence from the other end and is the reason the turn-cap table
re-derived this run states its own window and the eight seats it could not
measure.

It is also the third appearance of the class the ExO charter named on
2026-10-11 as a check that cannot see. The first was scope, `--limit 40`
over a seven-day window. The second was tooling, a code search returning
`total_count: 0` for an unindexed repository. **The third is source, and it
is the worst of the three, because scope and tooling at least return
something a reader can doubt.** A retired source returns a clean bill of
health.

**The rule that comes out of it, and it is new.** A check has a scope, a
tool and a source, and correcting any one of them does not test the other
two. The 2026-10-11 run fixed this section's scope and shipped it with the
source already dead for six days in the future; the 2026-10-18 run wrote a
whole section of the ExO charter explaining that decision 056 had retired
the seat workflows, and left the two commands above it and below it pointed
at them. **A correction written as a new paragraph does not reach the
paragraphs around it.** The mechanical form is cheap and it is now in both
charters: when a runtime, provider or surface is retired, grep every charter
for the commands that read it before the run ends, and report the count.

**The sweep, run this time.** Eleven references across twelve charters.
`prompts/exo-agent.md` held six, three of them dead instructions and one
dead-in-part; `prompts/pm-agent.md` held four, two of them dead and the
dispatch count dead; `prompts/engineer-agent.md` one dead-in-part;
`prompts/security-agent.md` one dead. `gh run list` for `checks.yml` and
`deploy-main.yml` is alive and was kept in all four. Zero charters named the
board's run record before this pull request.

**Fixed in this pull request.** ExO §2a-0 rewritten onto the board read, §2b
given the three non-success predicates a host run actually fails with, §2c's
presence metric replaced with the trigger ratio and the brief's two counts.
PM §1f given the board read and the three predicates, and its cap ratio
pointed at the manifest for the denominator. Engineer and security charters
corrected in one line each. The relay entry is marked answered.

**What is not fixed, and it is HQ's.** The board's run route takes no query
string; any parameter returns `{"error": "no such route"}`, and it returns a
fixed count of recent runs, 25 on 2026-10-24. Twenty-five rows reached back
six days this week and would reach back under two on 2026-10-23 alone, which
had seventeen runs. **A receipt scoped by count is the defect of 2026-10-11
rebuilt in the surface that fixed it.** The ask is on the relay page. Also
HQ's: `pr_url` and `report` are wrong for the crashed exo run, which is
recorded as "no pull request" and had opened #404 two minutes earlier, so the
one field a reader would use to judge whether work survived is the one field
that lies.

**Blameless note.** No seat skipped a step and HQ did the thing it was asked
to do. The gap is that an answered ask has no reader. A relay entry is
written by the seat that needs it and marked delivered by the chair, and
there is no third state for "granted", so the grant arrived as a silent
capability. The charter edit that closes this is one sentence in §2a-0: an
ask that is granted is a charter edit falling due, and the run that notices
rewrites the sections written around its absence in the same run. Ban list
checked on this entry.

## INC-2026-10-23-the-drift-guard-answered-green-from-a-checkout-that-could-not-see — every agent seat clones one commit deep, so the alarm for a production image eight days stale read "pending, inside the window" for all of them (2026-10-23, engineer seat, message run)

Recorded under the standing rule. This is the third entry on one shape: a
guard that could not measure something reported a verdict instead of saying
so. `INC-2026-10-14-the-two-apps-the-drift-guard-could-not-see` is the same
surface reading "unmeasured" where it should have read "behind", and company
standard L-A21 is the general rule, that a gate which saw nothing must not
read as a quiet pass. Today it is the same surface again, in the opposite
direction, reading "fine" where it should have read "I cannot tell".

**What happened, measured rather than reasoned.** The same tree, the same
`deploy_runtime` rows, the same minute. Run against a `git clone --depth 1`
checkout, `tools/delivery_health.py --surface deploy` answered:

    ok  deploy  a deploy is pending and still inside the 24h window:
                distill (0.1h), ingest (0.1h), weekly (0.1h)

Run against the same checkout after `git fetch --unshallow`, it answered:

    FAILING  deploy  the deployed code is not origin/main: distill is 7.9 days
                     behind; ingest is 7.3 days behind; weekly is 8.2 days behind

`weekly` is the press. The reproduction is two commands and it is in
`tests/test_deploy_drift.py` as
`test_a_checkout_that_cannot_place_the_image_is_not_a_green_deploy`.

**The mechanism, in one paragraph.** `undeployed_commits` recovers the
deployed commit by replaying each app's file digest backwards over history
until one matches the digest the container reported. A shallow clone has one
commit, so the replay matches nothing and returns a `why` with no commits.
`drift_began` then falls back to `changed_at`, the newest commit to the app's
files, which in a one-commit clone is that single commit and is minutes old.
The age comes out near zero, the age is inside the 24 hour grace window, and
the app is filed as a pending deploy.

**Why nobody caught it.** The fallback itself is deliberate and its docstring
argues for it correctly: a guard that cannot date a drift should under-report
rather than invent one. That argument is about the number. Nothing in it is
about the state, and the state is what every reader reads. The fixture that
covers the pending-deploy case recorded a digest matching no commit
(`"0ldc0dec0de"`), which is the shallow-clone shape rather than the
recent-merge shape, so the test that should have caught this was asserting the
bug. It has been rewritten to record the digest of the commit before the edit,
which is what a real deploy's row holds an hour after somebody merges.

**What it cost.** `tools/drift_watch.py` exists to put this alarm on the board
because the email path could not. It reads `state`, correctly, and filters to
`failing`. So from the day it shipped on 2026-10-17 it has run only from
sandboxes that clone one commit deep, found nothing failing, exited 0 green,
and posted no card, while three production jobs drifted past a week. The two
guardrails were each right about what they measured and the pair was blind.

**The fix.** An undated drift whose fallback clock lands inside the window is
`unknown`, not `ok`. One past the window still alarms, which is the old
under-reporting behaviour and is unchanged. `drift_watch` already exits 2 and
posts nothing on an `unknown` surface, so a shallow run now goes red and says
the comparison is what failed.

**The same reading, found in the same run on the till.** `check_checkout`
returned `failing` when the pricing page could not be reached at all, so any
sandbox with no egress would have posted a card saying the shop was shut on a
morning it was open. `check_compute` had read the identical silence as
`unknown` since the day before, with a test named
`test_a_request_that_never_arrived_is_unknown_not_failing`. The rule existed,
in this file, one function away, and the surface next to it did the opposite.
Fixed in the same pull request.

**What the org should take from it.** Both halves here are a guard reporting
a verdict about production from a checkout that could not reach the evidence.
The cheap question nobody asks of a new guard is which of its inputs the
runtime actually has. Every seat runs shallow, and no guard in this repository
says anywhere what depth of history it needs.

## INC-2026-10-23-the-ship-first-rules-closing-half-went-unrun-for-the-second-time — the same empty draft, five days old instead of two, and only a standing message in the wake remembered it (2026-10-23, engineer seat, message run)

Recorded under the standing rule. The first entry is
`INC-2026-10-18-the-ship-first-rules-closing-half-went-unrun-and-an-empty-draft-aged-two-days`
and this is the identical pull request, three days further on.

**What happened.** #358 opened at 02:26 UTC on 2026-10-18 with six lines, a
run note stub, and a body saying it would be filled in before `gh pr ready`.
It never was. The run that opened it ended without readying it and without
closing it. It was still open, still draft, still six lines, at 23:30 UTC on
2026-10-23, and GitHub will not merge a draft at all, so no gate could reach
it and no amount of review queue grooming could have moved it.

**What actually remembered it.** Not the repository, which holds no liveness
for a pull request. Not the board, although a card was opened about it on
2026-10-18 and sat in Review for five days. The thing that brought it back was
the standing paragraph appended to this seat's wake message, which is a
mechanism outside the repository entirely and which says so in its own words:
"this message is the only thing that remembers."

**Why the first entry's fix did not fire.** It proposed `tools/stale_drafts.py`
and that proposal is in the ledger at status `proposed`, which means no seat
may pick it up. The correction was written down and the thing that would
enforce it was gated behind an approval, which is incident 20's shape: a
register with a gate that decides something gets written and no gate that
decides it gets checked.

**Resolved rather than only filed.** The stub was merged into this run's
branch, the work it owed was built, and the older pull request was closed by
its own author with the containment proof the charter requires. The board card
was commented on and moved to Done. What remains open is the detector, and it
remains open because it needs the owner to move one ledger entry from
`proposed` to `accepted`.
