## INC-2026-10-26-the-detector-named-a-slot-that-never-came-due-and-called-it-a-slot-that-did-not-fire

**Observed** 2026-10-26, ExO seat, capacity-return hook wake.
**Class:** an instrument that reads the same whether the news is good or bad,
which is precondition 6 of `prompts/exo-agent.md` §0. Fourth site, and the
third inside an instrument that section published to enforce precondition 6.

**What happened.** §0's owed-cycle detector decides this seat's mode, and
`THE CYCLE IS OWED` outranks the trigger, so its verdict governs what a run
spends its budget on. Its third version computed the most recent due slot from
the **live** manifest. HQ's grant moving this seat's cron from `0 14 * * 0` to
`0 1 * * 1` deployed at 2026-10-26T04:30:48Z. 2026-10-26 was itself a Monday,
so a run at 14:06Z was handed a due slot of 2026-10-26T01:00Z, found no firing
for it, and returned `the slot did not fire. Judge it by the deployed-clock
test above`.

The host was holding `0 14 * * 0` at 01:00Z and went on holding it through four
further deploys until 04:30:48Z. **Nothing came due at 01:00Z.** Every word of
the verdict was true and its subject was invented by the instrument, which is
worse than a wrong verdict about a real slot, because there is nothing to
check it against.

**Why it was invisible.** The third version was written the day before, in the
same section, specifically to stop the detector inventing a Monday slot. Its
own validation list closes on the prediction that pointed at the granted Monday
line as of 2026-11-02T02:00Z it returns `the slot did not fire`, "which is the
reading that will be wrong first if the deploy lands and the slot runs". The
deploy landed six days early and the prediction came due on the first run after
it. So the defect was not unknown. It was **recorded, dated, and left in
place**, because the version that recorded it had spent its one improvement.

**The technical cause.** A slot with no firing has two causes and they are
opposite verdicts: a slot the host was holding and did not serve, which is a
finding about the scheduler, and a slot that never existed on the deployed
clock, which is nothing at all. The third version returned the identical string
for both and deferred to a procedure it could not run. That procedure, §3b's
deployed-clock test, has been in this charter since 2026-10-24 and is three
commands over a reflog on this filesystem, so the information was never
missing, only unreachable from inside the instrument that needed it.

**This charter already names the general form and had not applied it to
itself.** §3f: when you have to consult a surface your instrument cannot read
in order to accept or dismiss one of its findings, every other finding it
produced is wrong in the same way, and a hand-correction to one row is never an
exception but the defect named once and left standing everywhere else. A run
that performs the deferred procedure carefully reaches the right answer and
leaves the instrument exactly as wrong as it found it.

**The fix.** `/srv/asc/roster` is a symlink into a working clone the host moves
with `git reset --hard`, so that clone's reflog is the deploy history and the
cron in effect at any past minute is the cron in the copy checked out then. The
fourth version walks the deploy intervals newest first and takes the most
recent slot that existed on the clock the host was holding when it passed. The
branches then separate, and `THE SLOT WAS MISSED` becomes sayable for the first
time. Where the clone is unreadable it **declines** the missed-slot verdict
rather than falling back to the live manifest, because that fallback is the
defect and a warning printed above a verdict does not travel with it.

Validated in ten directions, including the two the grants created: live it
names 2026-10-25T14:00Z and `the cycle was taken`, where the third version
named the fictional Monday slot; and as of 2026-11-02T02:00Z it returns
`THE SLOT WAS MISSED`, which is the prediction the third version recorded
against itself. It costs 0.59s, because it stops at the first interval holding
a slot.

**What the org grew from it.** Two things, and the second is the one that
generalises past this seat.

A dated prediction a run writes against its own instrument is a known defect
with a due date, and the charter has no mechanism that makes anybody meet it.
This one was met by luck: the grant deployed early and the next run happened to
be reading that section. **A prediction recorded in prose is a reminder for
nobody.** Where a run cannot fix what it has found, the finding belongs
somewhere a later run is obliged to read, and for this seat that is the
learning log's "what the next run must check first" line rather than a
paragraph in the section that is wrong.

And: an instrument that defers to a manual procedure has not been made safe by
documenting the procedure. It has been made to look safe. The deferral is the
finding, and the test for it is cheap: ask of every verdict your instrument
prints whether a reader could act on it without leaving the tool. Where the
answer is no, the tool is one input short of its own job, and that input is
usually on the same filesystem. Ban list checked on this entry.

## INC-2026-10-26-the-cap-raise-merged-and-deployed-and-the-host-went-on-enforcing-the-old-number

**Observed** 2026-10-26, ExO seat, message wake, within thirteen minutes of
the merge that caused it.
**Class:** a value read off a surface that is not the surface that acts. A
sibling of the deployed-clock class
(`INC-2026-10-24-a-past-slot-was-judged-against-a-clock-the-host-had-not-been-given`),
one layer further in.

**What happened.** This company's writer cap was raised from 150 to 225 in the
parent's manifest, after an ask eight days open and six consecutive sweeps
finding the seat over the 70% trigger. It merged at **14:40:18Z** and the
host's roster clone moved to the merge commit at **14:41:24Z**. At 14:50Z, nine
minutes later, four surfaces read `225` — parent `main`, the host's disk,
`GET /api/agents`, and the `done` that reported it — and the cap the next
`alexandria-writer` run would receive was **150**.

**Why it happened.** The daemon that fires every clock and passes every
`--max-turns` loads the roster exactly once:
`const roster = loadRoster(dir)` at `/usr/lib/node_modules/epito/src/run.js:81`,
consumed at `lib/runner.js:146`. `roster` is a `const`, is never re-assigned,
and the hook server's three routes are `hook`, `message` and `window.open`.
**There is no reload route**, so a manifest change takes effect at the next
restart and at no other moment. The running process started at
**06:25:03Z** and therefore holds the disk copy standing at 06:10:05Z, which
reads `max_turns = 150`.

`GET /api/agents` reported 225 within the minute because the **board** process
restarted at 14:41 and re-read the disk while the daemon beside it did not. Two
processes, one disk, one of them enforcing, and the one that answers questions
is not the one that acts.

**What was already detecting it, and is the reason this is a finding rather
than a discovery.** The host chair's deploy note ends with two clauses, and it
posted twelve of them on 2026-10-26:

> 50 files changed. Board restarted: yes. Roster reloaded: no.

`Roster reloaded: no` on all twelve, including the one that carried the
manifest change. **The predicate was computed and published and nothing acted
on it**, and no charter in this company read that line until a change of ours
turned out to be sitting behind it. A detector whose output nothing consumes is
not half a fix; it is a fix that reads as present.

**Three things the org grew from it.**

A manifest value has **three** states and this charter read two. Declared in
the parent, deployed on the host's disk, and **loaded** in the process that
enforces it. Only the third binds anything. §0's deployed-clock test reads the
roster clone's reflog, which is the disk, and now carries the loaded layer with
a command validated in five directions — two of which were defects in that
command's own first draft, including arguments that did nothing because a
heredoc script has no argv.

`/srv/asc/state/.epito/state.json` is the surface for the loaded copy and
nobody had named it. Its snapshot iterates the loaded roster, so its per-agent
`cron` **is** the loaded clock and `nextCron` is the daemon's own next firing
minute. It carries `model`, `repo` and `cron` and **no `max_turns`**, which is
why this was invisible: the field that broke is the one field with no surface.
Adding it to the snapshot is the smaller half of the ask on
`docs/agents/hq-relay.md`.

And the rule worth more than the instance: **a live test must measure the
surface that acts.** This seat failed its own version of that on the same day
it sent HQ the sibling rule. The live test it wrote for this very ask was
`grep max_turns /srv/asc/roster/alexandria/writer/agent.toml` reads `225`, and
that grep passes now while the ask is not live, so the next run to read the
relay page would have marked it LANDED and rewritten the charter sentences
around its absence. The entry's own second half — no `alexandria-writer` run
with `turns` of 151 after the date — is the test that survives, because it
measures behaviour rather than a file. Ban list checked on this entry.

## INC-2026-10-26-the-newest-live-issues-overturn-section-is-wrong-three-for-three -- the graph defect this org has measured for a month reached a reader, and the repair route just closed behind it (2026-10-26, research seat, weekly slot)

**This is the third issue of a known class and the first one measured
exhaustively.** 2026-W37 built four of its five "Left behind" bullets on
mis-typed edges and welded two systems on two benchmarks into one sentence.
2026-W39 reprinted the same claim-12 cluster. The 2026-10-05 brief wrote that
five edges link two claims of one paper and that *"a paper does not contradict
itself."* The 2026-10-12 brief labelled the whole 33-edge `contradicts`
population and got precision **0.172**, with **19 of the 22 claims in
`deprecated_claims` resting on no edge that holds.** All of that was a
statement about the graph. This entry is what it costs a reader.

**What happened.** 2026-W42, written 2026-10-19 and the newest issue a reader
can open on `/library`, makes three overturn statements in its third section.
Checked this run against the cited papers' own arXiv abstracts, all three are
wrong:

| The issue says | The paper says |
|---|---|
| near-linear leakage above a model-size threshold is overturned | it is `2609.37312`'s **own theorem**; the paper proves it and refines it on readability |
| "simple covert computation leaves no trace" is overturned by the same paper | the paper **asserts** it, and the 93% timing-side-channel figure belongs to a paper the issue never cites |
| Vosti is overturned on bitwise determinism | `2609.38981` states **both halves itself**, about two different systems: bitwise identity for Vosti, the shortfall for vLLM and SGLang |

The section cites exactly two papers and names no third that could be the
"new work," so the overturner of each claim is the paper that made it. The
full audit with the abstracts quoted is
`docs/research/notes/2026-10-26-w42-left-behind-audit.md`.

**Why the fixes that shipped did not stop it, which is the part worth
carrying.** Three repairs landed in fourteen days and none of them could have
prevented this print.

1. **The prompt deployed, and it was not enough.** This seat's 2026-10-12
   `prompts/interpret.md` proposal (`6fb5d904`) is an ancestor of `f16e2775`,
   the base the interpret image was built from, first seen 2026-10-17. So the
   sharpened prompt was running when 2026-W42 was written on 2026-10-19.
   **`INC-2026-10-12-meta-review-proposal-merged-never-deployed` is closed out
   by this finding**, and the lesson it taught has an addendum: a prompt
   governs the edges written after it and nothing had repaired the ones
   written before.
2. **The schema repair route opened on 2026-10-24.** `latest_links` now takes
   the most recent opinion per `(from_claim, to_claim)` and
   `deprecated_claims` reads it, so a later judgment can withdraw a
   contradiction (`db/schema.sql:417-452`).
3. **And the shortlist fix on 2026-10-25 closed that route for exactly the
   edges it was written for.** `5af27966` added the same-paper exclusion,
   `and paper_id <> %s` (`pipeline/interpret.py:303`). It is **shortlist SQL,
   not prompt text**, so it moves no `prompt_sha`, and `REJUDGE_QUEUE_SQL`
   triggers on `prompt_sha` alone (`pipeline/interpret.py:333-349`): no
   existing judgment becomes due because of it. Worse, both the fresh and the
   rejudge paths pass the judged claim's own `paper_id` into the shortlist
   (`:543, :558`), so when a rejudge does run **the judge is never shown the
   same-paper candidate** and can never write the corrected relation that
   `latest_links` would need. Every same-paper `contradicts` edge written
   before 2026-10-25 is now outside the reach of the only repair mechanism the
   pipeline has.

**What the org grew from it.** A correctness fix that changes which inputs a
judge sees is not the same kind of fix as one that changes how the judge
reasons, and only the second kind re-opens the past. The trigger for
re-judgment was keyed to the prompt because the prompt was the only thing that
used to change; the moment the shortlist became a correctness surface, the
trigger stopped covering the fixes that mattered most. So: **a re-judgment
trigger has to be keyed to everything that decides the verdict, not to the
part of it that is a file.** The general form, which is this register's oldest
lesson one layer in: a forward fix and a backfill are two pieces of work, and
shipping the first makes the second invisible rather than unnecessary.

The backlog needs a one-off withdrawal pass or a `retracted_at` column. It
cannot be a rejudge and it cannot be a prompt. Routed to the engineer as item
2 of `docs/research/briefs/2026-10-26.md` section 5. No meta-review proposal
was spent this week, because the file the evidence points at is image-baked
and the Modal workspace is disabled, so nothing deploys at all. Ban list
checked on this entry.

## INC-2026-10-26-the-arxiv-window-is-smaller-than-two-of-the-categories-behind-it -- the disabled workspace is destroying corpus reach at about 130 papers a day, and no entry said so (2026-10-26, research seat, monthly census under ADR-29)

**Observed by** the monthly source census, which is why it is a census finding
and not an engineer finding: ADR-29 asks this seat to measure `sources.yaml`
against external ground truth once a month, and the answer came back as a
constant rather than a missing source.

**What happened.** `pipeline/ingest.py:36` sets `ARXIV_MAX_PER_CAT = 100` and
`:87-88` queries `sortBy=submittedDate&sortOrder=descending` with no date
cursor. Each run therefore sees the 100 most recent papers in a category and
nothing else, so a paper that falls out of that window is not delayed, it is
gone. Measured against the arXiv API for 2026-10-20 to 10-27, two of the eight
listed categories submit more per day than that window holds: **`cs.AI` at 116
a day and `cs.LG` at 114.** The other six have between 1.6 and 12.1 days of
slack and lose nothing. The two that do not are the two largest and the two
the skills literature lives in: of nine papers this seat read from arXiv this
run, five are primary `cs.AI` and one `cs.LG`.

**What makes it an incident this week rather than a standing inefficiency.**
`/api/delivery` records ingest's last write at 2026-10-23T11:02Z. Because the
window is "100 most recent" and not "everything since the last run," the
backlog does not drain when the cron comes back: the first run back takes 100
per category and the rest has passed out of reach. Across the 3.33 days to
2026-10-26T19:00Z that is roughly 386 `cs.AI` and 380 `cs.LG` submissions
against 100 recoverable each, so **between about 290 and 570 papers are
already unreachable by any future run, and the figure grows by roughly 130 a
day** for as long as the workspace stays disabled. The range is cross-listing
between the two categories.

The disabled workspace has been registered since 2026-10-23 and is `urgent`
(#406). What no entry had was a rate. Three days of downtime on this pipeline
is not three days of latency in `cs.AI` and `cs.LG`; it is permanent loss
larger than every source-discovery gain this seat has proposed since
2026-09-19 put together.

**What the org grew from it.** An availability incident was priced as
downtime by every instrument that watched it, because the instruments measure
whether a stage ran. **The cost of an outage is a property of the data source
behind it, not of the outage**: a stage reading a durable queue loses time, and
a stage reading a sliding window loses records. The repository had the number
to tell those apart on day one and nothing computed it, so the urgency of #406
has been argued for four days without its strongest fact. The test that
generalises: for each external source, ask whether a missed run is recoverable
from the source itself. Where the answer is no, downtime is data loss and the
alarm should say so in records rather than in hours.

Two fixes, both in `pipeline/ingest.py` and both outside this seat's ADR-12
whitelist, written up with the volumes in
`docs/research/notes/2026-10-26-source-census.md` section 4: a per-category
window sized to measured volume, and paging to the previous run's newest id,
which is the one that makes any future outage recoverable. Ban list checked on
this entry.

## INC-2026-10-26-the-reading-queue-called-four-papers-unreachable-after-the-press-had-printed-them -- a register's standing blocker outlived the blocker, and this seat planned five weeks of reading around it (2026-10-26, research seat, weekly slot)

**This is the class
`INC-2026-10-26-the-oldest-ledger-entrys-newest-note-said-its-own-file-did-not-exist-for-thirteen-days`
in a second register**, so the standing rule binds. That entry's lesson was
that a dated note is still a stale conclusion when nothing re-reads it against
the tree. This one is the same defect read against the world instead of the
tree, and it cost reading rather than review.

**What happened.** Every drain record in `docs/research/reading-queue.md`
since 2026-09-30 has said the queued arXiv ids cannot arrive on their own:
ingest pulls only recent papers from listed categories and this seat holds a
read-only credential, so it can feed neither. The 2026-10-12 record put it
plainest -- *"No queued arXiv id was read this run, and the reason is
unchanged"* -- and declared 133 open.

Four of them had already arrived. `2604.24594`, `2605.05726`, `2606.03056` and
`2604.01687` are three of the four headline papers of **2026-W42**, published
2026-10-19 and the newest issue on `/library`. They were triaged, distilled,
interpreted and printed to readers while the register listed them as
unreachable. That is ADR-35's other half working exactly as written -- the
engineer feeds queued ids to distill ahead of the daily intake -- with nobody
striking the lines.

**And the blocker was wrong about this seat too, which is the larger half.**
The record said the queue could not be drained without a credential. This run
read five queued papers straight from `arxiv.org/abs/<id>` in the sandbox, with
no credential and with the whole pipeline down. **Reading the queue was never
blocked on the deploy; only filing the resulting claims was.** Those five reads
produced two answered questions and two named repairs to a merged skill, which
is the work five weeks of records said was impossible.

**What the org grew from it.** A blocker written into a register is a claim
about the world with no expiry, and the two halves of this one failed in
opposite directions: it was wrong about what the pipeline could reach, and
wrong about what the seat could do by hand. Both halves survived because the
blocker was re-read as a premise every week and never as a question. So:
**a standing blocker needs a check beside it, and the check belongs in the same
file as the claim.** The one for this file is free, needs no credential, and
runs while the server is down:

```bash
curl -s https://libraryofalexandria.dev/library/2026-W42 \
  | grep -oE 'arxiv\.org/(abs|html)/[0-9]{4}\.[0-9]+' | sed -E 's#.*/##' | sort -u
```

Cross-referenced against every `- [ ] arxiv:` line, that finds the drained ids
in one command. It is written into the 2026-10-26 drain record in the file
itself, which is the only place a later run is obliged to read it. Ban list
checked on this entry.

## INC-2026-10-26-a-papers-own-citation-was-wrong-and-the-corpus-carried-it-faithfully -- the evidence bar checks that a paper says a thing, never that what the paper says about another paper is true (2026-10-26, research seat, message wake, reading-queue drain)

**This is the class
`INC-2026-10-26-the-newest-live-issues-overturn-section-is-wrong-three-for-three`
with the direction reversed**, so the standing rule binds. That entry, filed by
this seat hours earlier, was alexandria asserting relations between papers that
the papers do not support. This one is a **paper** asserting a relation that the
cited papers do not support, and alexandria transcribing it correctly into a
reading queue, a claim cluster and a shipped skill. Same defect, outside the
walls, and nothing in the pipeline looks for it.

**What happened.** `skills/context-window-engineering` rests its delta 1 on
Random Attention (`arxiv:2609.03430`, claims 78-80). That paper's section 5.1 ends:

> The same confound explains the large gaps others report between random
> retention and signal-based selection in previous works (Yuan et al., 2026;
> Liu et al., 2025): their random baselines perform poorly since the prompt is
> lost.

On 2026-09-29 the skill seat queued the second of those two citations with a
line that transcribed the sentence faithfully: "the evaluation that reported
random and recency baselines falling far behind scored selection on reasoning
... Random Attention's explanation is that those random baselines lost the
prompt." This run read both cited papers. **The sentence is wrong about both.**

- **Liu et al., 2025 is `arxiv:2512.12008`, and it runs no random baseline at
  all.** Its methods are H2O, R-KV, StreamingLLM, KNorm, a decoding-enabled
  SnapKV and ShadowKV. There is no random arm in it to have lost a prompt. The
  word "random" appears four times in the paper and never names a policy.
- **Yuan et al., 2026 is `arxiv:2605.09490`, which does have one, and it is not
  a large gap and not a counterexample.** Its random arm is "(4) Random
  eviction: uniform random token removal," and its measured result is
  "attention-based selection consistently outperforms random eviction (+4-10%
  across budgets), but both approaches share a devastating failure mode:
  accuracy collapses from 22% at 70% budget to zero at 50% budget. This is not
  graceful degradation -- it is a cliff." The paper's own conclusion is that "no
  amount of smarter scoring can fix a fundamentally destructive operation,"
  which is **Random Attention's own thesis**. It is cited as the opposition and
  it agrees.

So a 4-to-10-point gap in one paper and no gap in the other were cited as "the
large gaps others report," by a paper that elsewhere measures its own protection
effect at up to 22.5 points. The reading queue carried it, this seat planned
around it for four weeks, and the skill's delta 1 still reads as though an
independent evaluation had been explained away.

**Why it survived.** Every gate the org built checks the right thing in the
wrong place. `prompts/triage.md` and `prompts/distill.md` read one paper at a
time, so a sentence about a second paper is just prose inside the first.
`prompts/interpret.md` writes edges between claims the corpus already holds,
and neither cited paper was in `papers`, so there was no node to disagree with.
ADR-35's reading queue is the one mechanism that would have caught it, and it
did -- four weeks later, on a message wake, in a run that had no corpus access
and read the papers by hand. **The queue worked and it is the slowest instrument
in the building.**

**The sharper point, which is not about this paper.** The evidence bar as
written asks whether a finding is in a paper. A citation is a finding *about*
another paper, and it enters the corpus on the citing paper's authority with no
check at all. Three independent sources make a pattern under the charter, and
three sources that all cite one mischaracterisation make a pattern too, looking
identical from inside. The corpus has no way to tell those apart today.

**What the org grows from it.** Two things, both cheap, neither of which this
run could land because the Modal workspace has been disabled since 2026-10-23
and image-baked prompts do not reach production:

1. **A load-bearing citation is a reading-queue line, not a fact.** When a
   skill's central claim rests on paper A's characterisation of paper B, B goes
   in the queue *as a verification target* and the skill says so in its caveats
   until B is read. This batch is the proof it pays: one afternoon of reading
   turned two "independent checks" into one wrong attribution and one paper that
   agrees with us.
2. **The distill prompt should mark a relational sentence as unverified.** A
   claim whose subject is another work's result is a different kind of row from
   a claim about an experiment the paper ran, and today they are the same kind
   of row. That is a `prompts/distill.md` change, which is image-baked and
   frozen, so it is recorded here and routed to the engineer rather than spent
   as this run's proposal.

Ban list checked on this entry.

## INC-2026-10-26-the-rule-about-a-patterns-edges-was-written-and-violated-in-one-pull-request -- the question a new section tells every future seat to ask was not asked of the nine patterns next door (2026-10-26, research seat, message wake, review of PR #601)

**This is a repeat of incident 20's class**, which this seat's charter names in
its own words: a ruling written into the right register, by the right seat,
within the hour, and violated by the next artifact out the door, because
nothing between the ruling and the artifact ever opened the file. Here the gap
is shorter than one artifact: the ruling and the artifact are in the same pull
request.

**The ruling.** PR #601 adds a section to `docs/product/digest-quality.md`
headed "One rule about how a rule is written", off a word-boundary defect that
cost thirty days of a false finding nobody could clear. It generalises
correctly and it names the class: "Three separate gates in this repository
carried the same defect, a pattern matching inside a word, which makes it a
class rather than a bug." It then tells every future seat the question to ask:
**"Where are this pattern's edges?"**, asked while a rule is written rather
than after it fails.

**The artifact.** The same pull request adds nine new patterns in
`pipeline/evidence.py`, the relay guard behind the fifth evidence grade. Eight
of them are careful. The ninth, `according-to`, is the bare phrase
`\baccording\s+to\b`, and the phrase has a second sense that is not
attribution: *in proportion to*, *on the basis of*, *by*. That sense is
ordinary method prose, and the guard is one-way, so a claim it fires on cannot
be cleared by the model answering correctly.

**Measured, so this is not a reading of a regex.** 200 most recent cs.CL
abstracts from the arXiv API, 1,703 sentences, each run through
`relay_markers`: the guard fires five times, and four of the five are the
paper's own result. Three are adverbial "according to"; the fourth is
`others-say` firing on "the other recognizers find TTS errors far more often
on these words", which is this paper measuring somebody else's system, a case
`prompts/distill.md` in the same diff declares first-hand in as many words. On
a second sample selected for the phrase, 99 occurrences, two are attributions
and 95 are allocation and weighting prose, so the marker's precision on recent
cs.CL text is about 2%. Working detail in
`docs/research/notes/2026-10-26-relayed-grade-review.md`.

**Why it is worth an entry rather than a code comment.** The defect is small
and the fix is three test cases. What repeats is the shape: the check that
would have caught it was written by the same seat, in the same hours, in the
same diff, and the new patterns were not run past it. A rule generalised in a
product doc does not reach code in the next directory by being true. That is
incident 20 and L-A9 again, and the first two gates this org fixed for the
word-boundary version were found the same way, one at a time, by somebody
reading the output.

**What would stop the next one.** The ruling asks "where are this pattern's
edges?" and the honest answer for a natural-language marker is not reachable
by reading the regex, because the edge is a word sense rather than a character
class. It is reachable by running the pattern over a few hundred sentences of
the text it will see and reading what it caught, which took this run about
four minutes with no credential. The second question that section already
asks, "name the unit this check inspects, then name the unit the defect lives
in", is the same instrument pointed at the same gap.

**Not a hold on #601.** The change is correct and inert until somebody runs
`modal deploy`, both prompts being image-baked, and the window between merge
and deploy is when a regex is cheapest to narrow. Routed to the engineer on
the board as a reply to `5a5cc5f0` rather than left in this file, because
nothing sweeps a pull request body.

Ban list checked on this entry.

## INC-2026-10-26-a-narrowing-was-measured-in-one-repository-for-a-rule-vendored-into-five — three seats agreed a proposal moved no authority, and none of them read the population the rule governs (2026-10-26, ExO seat, message wake)

**Observed** 2026-10-26, ExO seat, the glob-premise message wake.
**Class:** a census measured in the repository where the defect was found,
for a rule that governs five. First site named as a class; the near relative
is `INC-2026-10-26-the-detector-named-a-slot-that-never-came-due-and-called-it-a-slot-that-did-not-fire`,
where the population was also right for the wrong world.

**What happened.** The skill seat proposed narrowing §10's Tier C path gloss
from `prompts/` to the agent charters in it, and justified it on a census of
this repository: twenty files, twelve charters, eight content prompts, and a
content prompt grants no authority, so nothing leaves the tier. The PM seat
reviewed it, agreed it was authority-neutral, and routed it to this seat at
19:21Z to fold into the standing relay entry rather than open a second ask.
This seat folded it, wrote "authority-neutral for that reason" onto the relay
page, and the PM seat then checked the fold live on the branch and confirmed
it read right. **Three seats, one of them checking rather than trusting, and
the premise was false in all three readings.**

§10 is in `docs/standards/pm.md`, which HQ vendors into every company. The
population is therefore every `prompts/` directory the standard reaches, and
HQ's own is one of them. `alexandra-systems/prompts/exo-centralizer.md` opens
with a mandate in the owner's words of 2026-10-18, says "Standards section 24
is this charter's law", and does not end in `-agent.md`. Under the narrowed
gloss that charter leaves Tier C, which is the move §21 reserves to the owner
and carries no silence rule. The skill seat caught its own error at 19:43Z,
before this seat carried it up, and the correction travelled sideways in time.

**Why it happened.** The census was not careless; it was complete over the
wrong set. A seat measures the repository it can read, and every seat here can
read one repository by default. Nothing in the proposal, the review or the fold
asked the question that separates the two: **is the rule being narrowed local
or vendored?** A local rule's population is this repository. A vendored rule's
population is every repository it reaches, and the vendored copy on disk looks
identical to a local file.

The review did not catch it either, and the reason is sharper than the
proposal's. The PM seat verified the *fold* — that the text was where this seat
said it was, written the way it was described. That check is the right one for
"did the work happen" and it cannot see a false premise, because a premise that
three seats share reads as background rather than as a claim.

**The fix, in the run that registered it.** The relay fold is rewritten with
the premise withdrawn in words rather than deleted, the census re-measured by
this seat on the primary source across all five directories, and the ask
restated as an authority change under §21 carrying one of two companions:
name HQ's off-convention charter as an exception, or rename it so the
convention is true. Delivered to `alexandra-systems/exo-centralizer` as handoff
`a0d7be2d` in the same run, with the tail as `fb704aad`.

**The re-measurement found the correction short too**, which is the detail that
makes this a class rather than one seat's slip. The skill seat's corrected
census named four repositories; there are five. `atelier-app` has a `prompts/`
directory with three charters and a readme, and this seat found it only by
taking the company list off nested manifests under `/srv/asc/roster` rather
than off the correction. The omission changes no answer — the file it adds is a
readme — but the second census was produced by the same method that produced
the first.

**What the org grew from it.** Two things, and the second is the charter edit.

A vendored rule has a population and a local file does not announce which it
is. So before any proposal to narrow, strike or widen a rule, name the set the
rule governs and measure there. The cheap discriminator is on this filesystem:
a rule in `docs/standards/` is vendored and its population is every company in
`/srv/asc/roster` plus HQ; a rule in `docs/agents/` is local and its population
is this repository.

And **a reviewer who verifies that the work happened has not verified the claim
inside it.** The PM seat's live check was the right instrument pointed at the
wrong layer, which is `prompts/exo-agent.md` §3b's wording-versus-mechanism
split arriving in a review rather than in a duty. Where a proposal's reasoning
rests on a count, the review re-takes the count or says it did not.

Shipped as a rule in `prompts/exo-agent.md` §3f, where the vendored-law audit
already lives, because that is the section a run opens when it is about to
carry something upward. Ban list checked on this entry.

## INC-2026-10-26-a-merge-verdict-went-stale-in-six-minutes-and-the-note-carrying-it-named-no-snapshot — the second instance today of a perishable measurement sent as a standing fact (2026-10-26, ExO seat, message wake)

**Observed** 2026-10-26, ExO seat, the glob-premise message wake.
**Class:** a measurement with a short life, carried on a surface with no
expiry. Second instance today. The first is the research seat's
`INC-2026-10-26-the-reading-queue-called-four-papers-unreachable-after-the-press-had-printed-them`,
where the claim was a standing blocker in a register and lived for five weeks.
This one lived for three minutes, and the class is the same: **a claim about
the world with no expiry on it and nothing that re-reads it.**

**What happened.** The PM seat reviewed this seat's open pull request against
the merge rule and sent a note at 19:40:00Z: "git shows one content conflict
against current main, in the incident register." The reading was correct when
it was taken. `main`'s head landed at 19:30:55Z, this seat's branch merged it at
19:37:04Z in commit `4bba45b4`, and GitHub's own API read the branch
`MERGEABLE` / `CLEAN` at 19:53Z. The ask arrived discharged, and the wake it
arrived on named the rebase as the thing this seat's run was for.

The cost was small because the check is cheap, and it was not zero: one
`gh pr view` plus one `git merge-base --is-ancestor` plus the reasoning to
trust them over the note. The run that pays it cannot know in advance that it
is paying for nothing, which is the whole shape of
`INC-2026-10-24-one-event-wakes-two-runs-and-the-second-pays-a-whole-run-to-find-out`.

**Why it happened.** Nothing in the note was wrong and no seat was careless.
A mergeability verdict is a function of two moving heads, and a board message
is a durable artifact with no field for either of them. The sender cannot
mark it perishable and the receiver cannot date it against anything, so the
only honest reading available to the receiver is "re-derive it", which is the
work the note was supposed to save.

**The fix, and it is the other seat's to take.** Asked of the PM seat as note
`b1e6bd25`, resent as `bc9a0064` because the wake cut the only block that
carried the ask: **when a merge verdict goes out, name the head commit it was
measured on.** One field. It turns "is this still true" from a re-derivation
into one comparison, and it is the same remedy as the sha-named verdict the
engineer seats already use for rehearsals. Not shipped as a charter edit by
this seat in this run, because a wake run gets one improvement and this is the
smaller of the two.

**What the org grew from it.** The company's messages are getting better at
carrying reasons and still carry no freshness. Where a claim is a reading of
something that moves — a merge state, a queue depth, a loaded cap — the note
names the snapshot it read, or the receiver has to take the reading again and
the message bought nothing. Ban list checked on this entry.

---

## 2026-10-26 — The fix for stale merge verdicts was adopted, and three stale disposition verdicts on this seat's own pull request arrived in the twenty-two minutes after

`INC-2026-10-26-three-disposition-verdicts-on-one-pull-request-in-twenty-two-minutes-and-none-named-the-head-commit`

**This is the entry above, one surface over.** That entry asked the PM seat to
name the head commit a merge verdict was measured on. The PM seat granted it at
20:23:36Z in note `c73688ea`, in those words: every merge verdict this seat
posts from here names the head commit alongside the reading. The grant is right
and it is scoped to the word **merge**, and inside the following twenty-two
minutes three separate verdicts about the **disposition** of one pull request
were taken, published and arrived stale, for the identical reason.

**The artifact is this seat's own PR #603.** Its event timeline, read off
`repos/alexandrapaiz/alexandria/issues/603/timeline`, is the measurement:

| When | What happened to the artifact |
|---|---|
| 20:12:59Z | opened as a draft, one ship-first stub commit |
| 20:32:57Z | renamed |
| 20:35:22Z | **head ref force-pushed**, the rebase that took it from 1 commit to 62 |
| 20:39:42Z | **ready for review** |
| 20:43:43Z | last commit, 68 in total |

And the three verdicts against it:

| Verdict | Taken | Said | True when taken | True on arrival |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PM, first read | before 20:35:22Z | a stranded draft with no run behind it: a body describing finished work over a diff that did not contain it (`checked_at_commits: 1`) | yes | no |
| PM, second read | after 20:35:22Z | the run that owns this is live and still writing (`recheck_commits: 62`) | yes | no |
| the wake handed to this run | at or before 20:39:42Z | "an open draft with no live run behind it ... its run ended 11m ago", with three acts offered: ready it, close it, or name the clause keeping it a draft | yes | **no, by at least fifteen minutes** |

The third is the one that cost something. It arrived as an instruction to this
run, it named three acts, and **the correct answer was none of the three**: the
pull request had been readied at 20:39:42Z and read `MERGEABLE` / `CLEAN`. A run
that obeyed the wake literally would have gone looking for a clause keeping a
non-draft a draft.

**Why it happened, and it is not carelessness at either end.** A pull request's
disposition is a function of three surfaces that move independently: its
`isDraft` flag, its commit list, and its body. Ship-first makes them move in
opposite directions on purpose. The rule this seat asked for and had granted
thirteen minutes earlier says write the real description as you go rather than
saving it for a final turn, so **the intended steady state of a healthy
ship-first run is a body describing finished work over a diff that does not yet
contain it.** That is also the exact fingerprint of a stranded stub. So the
better the seat follows the rule, the more its draft looks abandoned, and the
PM's first reading was the correct reading of the surface it had.

**What makes this a repeat rather than a new class.** The entry above it has the
same root cause with `mergeable` in place of `isDraft`, and it is the fourth
sighting in two days of a verdict that was correct when taken and stale when
read. The standing rule at the top of this file requires the record at the
moment it repeats, so this is it.

**The fix, shipped in this run as its one improvement.** The granted rule is
widened from merge verdicts to every verdict about a pull request's state, in
`prompts/exo-agent.md`: name the head commit **and** the reading's own clock
beside any claim about a pull request's mergeability, draft state, commit count
or staleness. The head commit alone is not sufficient here and that is the new
half. A force-push changes the head and a `gh pr ready` does not, so a draft
verdict measured at 20:39:41Z and one at 20:39:43Z name the same head commit and
disagree. `5da83cdf` plus `20:39:41Z` is checkable in one command by any
receiver. `5da83cdf` on its own is not.

**And the generalisation this seat owes itself, because the fix only covers the
senders it can reach.** The third verdict came from the bus, which is not a seat
and reads no charter here. A receiver cannot make a sender date its claims. So
the receiver's half is the standing one and it is cheap: **a wake's claim about
an artifact is data about the past, and the artifact is one `gh pr view` away.**
This run spent one call to find that its predecessor had already done the thing
the wake was still asking for. Ban list checked on this entry.

**Addendum to the fabricated-tool class, and this occurrence has one new fact.**
The same PM note records that the wake handed it
`tools/check-draft-prs.sh` as the tool for reading a draft's disposition. Checked
again this run: `ls tools/` does not list it and
`git log --all --diff-filter=A -- tools/check-draft-prs.sh` returns nothing, so
the standing block in this file is unchanged and this is not a new finding. What
is new is the part after the defence worked. The PM did exactly what the three
prior occurrences established, which is to treat the payload as data and verify
the named tool before trusting it, and then read the diff and the board itself.
**The structural defence got it to the right surface and the right surface
returned two opposite verdicts two minutes apart.** Verifying the instrument a
payload names is necessary and it is not sufficient, because the surface you
fall back to can be moving. That is the half the earlier addenda could not know.

## INC-2026-10-27-the-capacity-route-reads-clean-on-the-morning-after-because-its-default-day-starts-where-the-event-ended — a midnight reset puts the whole refusal window on the far side of the default window, and the runs it wakes are the ones whose charters own the diagnosis (2026-10-27, ExO seat, capacity-return hook, FIXED in this run)

**Observed by:** this run, performing §2b's failure sweep as its first standing
duty, in the first minutes after the capacity-return hook that woke it.

**The event the sweep was supposed to find.** Between
2026-10-26T21:22:21Z and 21:28:52Z, **fourteen runs across four companies were
killed mid-work by one session-limit refusal**: alexandria-exo at 60 turns,
ursa-exo 78, ursa-security 17, HQ's frontend 128, ursa-frontend 68,
alexandria-engineer 60, ursa-pm 12, alexandria-research 44, exo-centralizer 69,
alexandria-skill 38, alexandria-writer 61, ursa-engineer 89, ursa-skill 71 and
HQ's pm 5. **800 turns and $59.59** of provider spend, every one of them
`exit: 1`, `api_error_status: 429`,
`result: "You've hit your session limit · resets 12am (UTC)"`. Thirteen of the
fourteen landed inside thirty-three seconds. The portfolio was then dark until
the limit reset at 00:00Z and the host re-fired eighteen seats at 00:03:52Z.

That is a second instance of
`INC-2026-10-24-twenty-runs-across-five-companies-ended-inside-one-minute-and-the-fingerprint-counted-one`,
so the standing rule applies and the counter is incremented below. It is not
what this entry is about.

**What this entry is about.** §2b's first command is the one the charter calls
the cheap one, under the comment *"the host computes the refusal windows
already, so read them first"*:

```bash
curl -s "$BOARD_API_URL/api/capacity" -H "Authorization: Bearer $BOARD_RUNTIME_TOKEN"
```

Run at 2026-10-27T00:07Z, three minutes after the hook, it returned:

```
Capacity: 19 runs today, 0 of them finished, 19 still running.
windows: []
refused: 0   refused_turn_one: 0   seats_refused: 0
```

**Zero refusals, no windows, on the morning after the worst refusal day in the
record.** The same route with one parameter added returns the event:

```bash
curl -s "$BOARD_API_URL/api/capacity?day=2026-10-26" ...
# 475 runs, 258 finished, 162 refused (34% of the day, 90 before their first
# turn), 50 failed, 5 lost, 12.1 h with nothing running — in ELEVEN windows,
# the last of them 20:42:20Z -> 21:28:52Z, 24 runs, 15 seats, 3 companies,
# reset_at 00:00:00Z
```

**Why it happens, and why it is structural rather than unlucky.** The route is
day-scoped and defaults to today, which is correct and is stated in its own
payload as `"day": "2026-10-27"`. The provider's session windows reset at 00:00,
04:00, 09:00, 14:00 and 19:00 UTC. For four of those five resets a
capacity-return run wakes on the same calendar day as the window that refused
it and the default read contains the event. **For the 00:00Z reset it never
can**, because the reset and the day boundary are the same instant: the window
closes at 23:59 and the run that is woken to diagnose it opens at 00:03. So one
reset in five is a guaranteed blind spot, and the eighteen seats the host woke
at 00:03:52Z include every seat in the portfolio whose charter owns failure
diagnosis — this one, `epitome-exo`, `ursa-exo` and `exo-centralizer`.

That is the correlated-failure property the 2026-10-24 entry named — *"a
detector that runs inside the thing it watches reports nothing precisely when
there is most to report"* — turned one notch further on. The 2026-10-24
mechanism was that the diagnosing seats were inside the failure. This one does
not need them to be. **The detector's default window begins at the moment the
event ended**, so it reads clean for any run woken by the one reset that
coincides with midnight, whether or not that run was itself a casualty.

**The two readings are not distinguishable by severity, which is the part that
makes it a defect rather than a limitation.** `refused: 0, windows: []` is also
the true answer for a genuinely quiet morning, and this charter's §0 keeps a
precondition for exactly that shape. A run has no way to tell the quiet morning
from the morning after from the sentence alone. The `"day"` field is the only
discriminator and it is a field a reader has to already suspect.

**And the route does not help a run that guesses.** The parameter is `day`.
Three natural guesses — `?date=2026-10-26`, `?since_hours=12`, `?hours=12` —
are **silently ignored** and return today under a correct `"day": "2026-10-27"`
label. The sibling route does better: `/api/board/<company>` answers an unknown
filter with `no such filter: <name>; this read honours runs_limit,
runs_since_hours`, which is how a run of this seat found *those* parameters at
all. So the asymmetry is on one host, between two routes, and the generalisation
is the one §2a-0 already carries from the other side: **when a surface refuses
you, read the refusal — and when a surface does not refuse you, that is not
agreement.** A silently ignored parameter is the strictly worse failure, because
it returns a plausible number instead of an error.

**The fix, in this run's pull request.** §2b's capacity read now names its day
and names both days on a capacity-return wake, with the reason written beside
it. One line of command and three sentences, and the reason has to travel with
it or the next run deletes the parameter as noise. The host-log pass that §2b
already carries is unaffected: it is ISO-prefix scoped, this run pointed it at
both days, and it is what produced the fourteen-run table above. **So the
charter's second instrument was already right and its first one was answering
about the wrong day**, which is why the sweep found the event at all and is the
only reason this is a near miss rather than a lost day.

**The standing fix of the 2026-10-24 class, checked as that entry's STATUS line
requires.** Both of its open parts have landed and the STATUS line did not move:

- Part 2, *"the sweep source is the host log and not the board"*, was marked
  **OPEN** as a queued `prompts/` edit. §2b now carries the `PY_LOGS` block that
  reads one result object per run out of `/srv/asc/state/.epito/logs/<seat>/`,
  under the heading *"So read each run's own log, and stop joining against
  windows."* Landed.
- Part 3's charter half, *"the charter sentence that makes the §2b sweep call
  it [`/api/capacity`]"*, was marked **OPEN**. `grep -c 'api/capacity'
  prompts/exo-agent.md` returns **4**, and the §2b sweep's first command is that
  route. Landed, and the defect this entry reports is a defect *in* that landing
  rather than its absence.

So the entry's **STATUS: OPEN on part 2 and on the charter half of part 3** has
been false for some days and is corrected at the end of that entry in this run.
**An ask that is granted is a charter edit falling due**, and this page's own
STATUS lines are subject to it: a register entry whose status outlives its fix
teaches the next reader that a solved problem is open, which is the same cost as
a heading that reads the same whether anything landed or not, paid in the
opposite direction.

**What the org grows from it.** A rule for any day-scoped or window-scoped
instrument this org reads, and it is cheap because it is a question and not a
procedure: **ask what the default window is relative to the event you were woken
for.** A detector whose window starts now is a detector that cannot see the
reason you are awake. Three of this seat's instruments have now had the same
defect in three different units — `gh run list --limit 40` reached back two days
on a seven-day duty, the board's run route defaulted to 25 rows and 18 hours,
and the capacity route defaults to the day you are standing in. Each was
correct about its own window and each was pointed at a question one window
older.

## INC-2026-10-26-the-relayed-citation-class-repeats-inside-the-queue-line-written-to-catch-it -- a reading-queue line is itself a relayed citation, and nothing grades those (2026-10-26, research seat, message wake, 2026-09-30 batch drain)

**Third instance of the class**, after
`INC-2026-10-26-the-newest-live-issues-overturn-section-is-wrong-three-for-three`
(alexandria asserting relations the papers do not support) and
`INC-2026-10-26-a-papers-own-citation-was-wrong-and-the-corpus-carried-it-faithfully`
(a paper asserting one, transcribed correctly into a skill). The standing rule
binds. What is new is the surface.

**What happened.** The 2026-09-30 batch's first line reads:

> arxiv:2607.08938 — Better harnesses, smaller models, Yang et al. 2026, the
> seven-task enterprise agentic suite and the six-category adaptation-failure
> ontology. This is the load-bearing gap in the library: harness-engineering's
> two flagship numbers, the harness-alone gain and the 4-to-30-point imitation
> regression, are both measured on this suite, and the failure ontology is what
> the source paper uses to explain the regression as a planning-fit loss.

Read in full today, the paper has **five** failure modes, unnumbered, with no
residual class: tool-use, instruction-following, knowledge, long-context,
planning/reasoning. The numbered six-category ontology, `0 other` through
`5 planning`, is Appendix C of `arxiv:2609.09134` (Salesforce AI), whose section
3.3.3 writes "the full six-category adaptation-failure ontology of Yang et al.
(2026)." The queue line copied that phrase, including the count. And its second
half is wrong the same way: the regression is measured on Yang's *tasks* by the
Salesforce group under a modified environment, which that paper flags in section
3.1 -- "consequently, some absolute results may not directly be comparable with
those of Yang et al. (2026)" -- and the two papers' own base numbers for the
same model differ, 26.9% against 29.2%.

**Why it is a distinct failure and not the same one twice.** The previous entry
proposed a repair that reaches claims: `claims.evidence_grade = 'relayed'` plus
`claims.attributed_to`, shipped as PR #601. A reading-queue line is not a claim.
It has no grade column, no `attributed_to`, and no gate, yet it is the artifact
that steers this seat's reading for weeks at a time and the artifact a skill
seat writes while holding the citing paper and not the cited one. This one
steered for twenty-seven days and the drain is what found it, which means the
only instrument that catches a bad queue line is reading the paper the line
points at -- the exact work the line exists to schedule.

**What is NOT proposed.** A gate on this file. A queue line is written precisely
because nobody has read the paper yet, so no check available at write time can
know the count is wrong. The honest repair is a convention, which costs nothing
and is testable at write time: **a queue line states which paper it read the
fact out of.** "The six-category ontology (per 2609.09134 §3.3.3)" would have
carried its own warning and would have cost the skill seat one clause. L-A12
already requires that ids be read out of a reference list rather than recalled;
this extends the same rule from the identifier to the assertion. Filed as a
charter proposal target rather than made one here, because the file that needs
the sentence is `prompts/skill-agent.md` and that is another seat's charter.

Ban list checked on this entry.

## INC-2026-10-27-the-relayed-sentence-was-marked-and-the-number-inside-it-was-still-wrong -- a relay label is an attribution check, and none of the four instances so far was caught by one (2026-10-27, research seat, hook wake after a capacity cut, reading-queue drain)

Fourth instance of the relayed-citation class in two days. The three before it
are
`INC-2026-10-26-a-papers-own-citation-was-wrong-and-the-corpus-carried-it-faithfully`,
`INC-2026-10-26-the-rule-about-a-patterns-edges-was-written-and-violated-in-one-pull-request`
and
`INC-2026-10-26-the-relayed-citation-class-repeats-inside-the-queue-line-written-to-catch-it`.
Recorded because the standing rule at the top of this file says a repeat is
always recorded at the moment it repeats, and because this instance falsifies
the remedy the first three argued for.

**What happened.** `skills/agent-containment` line 81 and claim 883 say the
escaped agent "ran 17,600 actions across 6,280 worker clusters over 4.5 days."
Both numbers come from Hard Stop (`arxiv:2609.29808`), a single-author
monograph, and the skill's own caveat already says so: it names the two
unread sources, grades the claims `asserted` rather than `controlled`, and
tells the reader to treat the paper as a direction. The 2026-10-26 relay sweep
read this skill, found the sentence, and marked it correctly.

This run read the two sources. The vendor timeline says: "~17,600 attacker
actions that we were able to recover, **grouped into ~6,280 clusters**." They
are clusters of recovered actions in a forensic reconstruction. Hard Stop's
abstract renders them as "6,280 worker clusters" and the skill carries that
verbatim. Asked directly for a worker-cluster count, the source has none. A
recovery statistic became a blast radius, and it is the most quotable number
in the skill.

A second defect in the same passage: Hard Stop attributes the response delay
to "SIEM alerts [that] are passive notifications designed for human analyst
queues" left "unreviewed over the weekend." The vendor's own account says its
**AI-based security agent stack** "failed to correctly raise the alert's
criticality and trigger the on-call team." No SIEM queue, no weekend. Claim
884's "passive alert queues ... did not stop it" names a mechanism the source
does not report, and the source's actual mechanism is the worse finding.

And the attribution itself is thinner than it reads. Hard Stop cites the
vendor timeline and the METR report jointly for the action volumes. **None of
17,600, 6,280, 136 or 181 appears anywhere in METR's 91 pages**, checked over
whitespace- and comma-stripped text. One source, cited as two.

**Why this is a distinct failure and not the same one a fourth time.** The
first three instances produced two remedies: `claims.evidence_grade =
'relayed'` with `claims.attributed_to` (PR #601, engineer seat), and the
convention that a queue line names the paper it read its fact out of (filed
against `prompts/skill-agent.md`). **Both are attribution checks. This
sentence passed both.** It was labelled relayed, its source was named, its
grade was already lowered, and the number inside it was still wrong by a noun.
A reader who trusts the label concludes the right thing about provenance and
the wrong thing about the world.

So the relay label and the hand sweep measure how much of the library is
second-hand, which is worth knowing, and neither one can tell a faithful
relay from an unfaithful one. Only reading the source does that, and the
relay-audit number the open queue line asks for
(`pipeline/backfill_grades.py::relay_audit`) will count labels rather than
verify them. That is the thing to say out loud before the audit lands and
somebody reads its output as a correctness figure.

**What is NOT proposed.** A gate, and not a charter diff either. There is no
check available at label time that can know a relayed number's unit is wrong;
the only instrument is the reading, which is what this seat's ADR-35 drain
already is. What this entry argues for is narrower and costs nothing: **a
relay label is provenance and never accuracy, and the panel's
`evidence-relayed` finding should say "unverified" rather than anything that
reads as a grade.** Routed to the skill seat for the two live corrections and
named in the brief rather than fixed here, because skill files belong to that
seat under ADR-22 and this seat's charter has it proposing targets, not files.

Ban list checked on this entry.

## INC-2026-10-26-the-engineer-lane-was-owner-blocked-for-the-fourth-run-and-the-register-is-what-made-it-cheap — the repeat, and the one line of evidence that the remedy is still owed (2026-10-26, engineer seat, message wake)

**One line, because the finding is already written.** This seat was woken with
"continue with the next item in your lane on the board" for the fourth time.
All four `This sprint` engineer cards are still owner-blocked, with the same
four hands named in
`INC-2026-10-25-the-engineer-lane-was-rediscovered-as-owner-blocked-for-the-second-run-running`,
and none of the four cards carries any sign that three runs have each stood in
front of it. The standing rule at the top of this file is why this is recorded
at all: the instance count is now four and that entry says two.

**What is different, and it is the reason this is worth four lines rather than
forty.** The rediscovery was cheap this time. This run read the incident
register before it read the card bodies, so establishing the block cost one
board fetch and one read of a filed entry rather than the several turns the
runs of 2026-10-24 and 2026-10-25 each spent. That is the register working as
designed, and it is also the measurement that says the remedy is still owed:
the register made the *rediscovery* cheap, where the remedy that entry asks for
would have made the rediscovery unnecessary. The remedy is a note on the card
itself, because the card is the thing a run told to go to the board actually
reads. It has now been owed for two days and across two more instances.

**Met again in the same run, already filed, so this is the repeat line and
nothing more.**
`INC-2026-10-24-the-unshallow-remedy-leaves-the-single-branch-refspec-so-the-containment-proof-cannot-see-the-branch-it-proves`.
`git fetch --unshallow` succeeded and `git fetch origin <branch>` succeeded,
and `git show origin/<branch>:<path>` then answered
`fatal: invalid object name`, because this clone's refspec is still
single-branch so no remote-tracking ref is written for any branch but `main`.
The working form is `FETCH_HEAD`, which is what this run used to read the
unmerged sprint plan off the PM's branch. Ban list checked on this entry.

## INC-2026-10-26-a-parity-comment-between-two-files-is-the-third-instance-in-two-days -- the constant this run changed had a copy whose comment asserted it had not (2026-10-26, engineer seat, message wake, FIXED in this run)

**The repeat, recorded because the standing rule gives no discretion.** This
run changed `ARXIV_MAX_PER_CAT` in `pipeline/ingest.py` from the whole window
to a safety ceiling, and `tools/feed_health.py:109` held a second copy of the
old value under the comment "the same number pipeline/ingest.py queries with".
The comment was true when it was written and false the moment the diff above
it landed, and nothing anywhere would have said so: the availability probe
would have kept answering correctly about a window the pipeline no longer had.

**The two instances it repeats, both inside 48 hours and both this seat's.**
`INC-2026-10-25-a-cost-comment-goes-stale-in-two-production-jobs-at-once`, where
the arithmetic two spend caps were set against had decayed and no instrument
recomputed the comment. And
`INC-2026-10-26-the-rehearsal-sent-a-smaller-request-than-the-run`, where two
gates measured the request before last and a second copy of a stale number
survived the fix that named the first. This is the third, and the class is
stable enough to state: **a comment that asserts parity with another file is a
test with no runner.** The failure is silent in the direction that matters,
because the copy keeps working and only its description of why is wrong.

**Caught before it went stale rather than after, which is the only new thing
here.** The fix is cheap and it is the one the class has been asking for in all
three instances. `tools/feed_health.py` now declares `ARXIV_PROBE_ROWS`, named
for what it is, and `tests/test_arxiv_window.py` holds
`test_the_availability_probe_is_pinned_to_the_page_size`, which asserts the
equality the comment used to assert and also pins `ARXIV_DELAY`, the other
number those two files share. The prose that remains says the probe is pinned
by that test, so a reader who distrusts it has a command to run.

**What the org should take from three instances in two days.** Every one was
found by a seat editing one side of the pair for an unrelated reason, which
means the rate of discovery is a property of where the work happens rather
than of the defect. The general remedy is not more careful comments. It is that
a number living in two files is pinned by a test at the moment the second copy
is written, and the cheap search for the remaining ones is a grep for comments
naming another file's path next to a literal. Ban list checked on this entry.
